subtopic: EXTENSION TO EMPLOYEES OF COMMISSIONS, ETC.  APPLICATION TO OFFENCES COM- MITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill will provide four amendments to the Official Secrets Act. First, it will extend the expression "office under His Majesty" to include employees of commissions, corporations and other agencies of the crown. Second, it will give an extraterritorial effect to the act by making it applicable to offences committed outside of Canada by Canadian citizens, or to persons who in another country have communicated information which they obtained during the time that they owed allegiance to Canada. Third, it will increase the penalties under the act, and fourth, it will also remove any doubt that persons charged under the act for offences against the act under part XV of the Criminal Code relating to summary convictions may be fingerprinted.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first

speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: $ 5,431,946 HEALTH AND WELFARE  "DIETARY DITTIES"
speechtext:
"Dietary Ditties", a little
humorous device for teaching simple nutrition lessons, appears regularly in Canada's Health and Welfare. It is written by members of the staff of the nutrition division, usually in their own time.
The cost of each illustration is approximately $20. It is impossible to estimate the cost of printing because it represents a very small fraction of the cost of producing a single page of the magazine by offset lithography.
Numerous requests have been received by the department for permission to republish "Dietary Ditties". For instance, the United States national publicity council for health and welfare services called attention in its monthly bulletin to this feature as an interesting way of teaching simple nutrition lessons; this resulted in a great many requests for use in house organs and health education publications. In Canada "Dietary Ditties" is

being used by a large number of weekly newspapers and house organs, such as Confederation Life Bulletin, Toronto; Hydro News (Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario); National Labour Journal, Ottawa; the house organ of the Rubfoerset Company Limited, Gravenhurst, Ontario, etc.

speechtext: How will the money be obtained that is required to carry out the operations under this bill? Will it come from the estimates submitted by the Department of Trade and Commerce, or from those of the Department of National Defence?

speechtext:
Since the inception of civilian buying the practice has been that the requisition is accompanied by a certificate of encumbrance on the estimates of the armed services. In other words, we get a requisition to procure a certain supply, and at the same time we get a certificate of encumbrance

Defence Supplies
from the- Department of National Defence making the cost of that supply a charge on the defense estimates.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext: Then the amounts would appear in the estimates for the present fiscal year under the Department of National Defence?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext: I wonder if the minister would now be good enough to answer the question I have asked previously. subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext: I do not think the minister should go on singing that old song. We understand each other, I think. I am now asking what there is the minister cannot do without the powers under the munitions and supply act, which would make this new legislation necessary. In other words, why can he not go into the market in the ordinary course of business and with the ordinary powers with which he is clothed? Why are these new powers necessary? I hope the minister will give me an answer and not fall back on that old hair-splitting device he has used. He is much too big for that.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.

speechtext: Well, I do not know that I care very much whether the discussion is on section 1 or on section 3, but I thought section 1 was the place to ask general questions, and I have already asked this question once or twice. subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext: What my hon. friend is asking is why the purchase of defence supplies requires any powers whatever, other than the power to make the purchase. I think that is wha't he has in mind. He speaks of new powers, but there are no new powers contained in this bill. I wish he would see eye to eye with me on that, because as a matter of fact the powers contained in this bill have been in the legislation under which the appropriate minister has been operating, and they are the only authority he has or has had for defence purchasing.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext:
You mean the Department of
Munitions and Supply Act?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes. Let us say we will depend upon the ordinary purchasing technique, and place a contract for a very urgent unit of defence. The position will be like any contract placed by the Department of Public Works or any other department; there is no way to compel delivery on time. Perhaps my hon. friend is not as familiar with government purchasing as I am, but I can assure him that there is a tendency on the part of contractors to feel that the government is a very good and kind client and will not be too rough if he does not finish on time, whereas the same contractor may have a private buyer who is pretty rough, so he will do the last mentioned job first. In other words the government is apt to take second place to private contractors if we do not have this power to demand priority. The same situation exists with respect to supplies. At the moment supplies are fairly easy and this legislation probably would not be needed at this time. If this market tightens up much more, however, it may be very difficult to carry out defence purchases unless we have the power to requisition raw materials.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext: I come back to the first point. The minister has said this is not necessary at this time, but I need not go over that again; as he says, the bill was given second reading yesterday. My comment on that would be, first, that I do not believe and I do not think anyone else in this house believes that anyone contracting or dealing with the Minister of Trade and Commerce would be inclined to proceed in that way, because the minister is a fairly forceful fellow, and he has a good deal of power. The second point, which I want to make as strongly as I can, is that if it were clear that the requirement of the minister was in connection with national defence, nothing would make me believe that there would be the difficulty which the minister represents. matter. I said the power to demand priority is needed at the present time. I said the power to requisition probably is not needed at the moment, but that we are moving into a tighter market and it might be needed at any time.
Defence Supplies

I know that, but my complaint is that we do not know the salaries paid to the officials of crown companies. I should like to have a chart showing the salaries and functions of the various officials of the Canadian Commercial Corporation as well as other crown companies. I am not an opponent of the government; I am a supporter of it. During the war and since, it has always been my stand in the house that the salaries paid these officials should be made known. We vote the money here, and we want to know how it is spent. These gentlemen may or may not be good, but at least we should know the amount that is paid to them by way of salary, or whatever it is called, and the amount that is paid for their travelling expenses.
I did receive a chart of another crown company showing the names of the personnel and their functions, but not their salaries. Why is it impossible to obtain that information? As a member of parliament representing a constituency in Canada I believe that all the members should be informed as to the amounts paid to civil servants, high or low.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext: And presidents and past presidents of railways.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.

That applies to the members of the hon. gentleman's group as well, because they did not insist on having that information. I am bound therefore by the decision of my colleagues who were members of that committee.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Surely that does not bind the rest of us in this house.

Defence Supplies

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext: It does not bind the rest of the house, but as a member of the committee I am informing the house what happened. It is all public knowledge. The members are free to ask whatever questions they desire, but in this matter I do not want anyone in the civil service to do otherwise than respect our parliamentary institutions and parliament as a whole. There seem to be two categories of people, members of parliament whose salary is mentioned in the newspaper as being too high, and men rendering a public service whose salaries are not disclosed. I am not attacking them, but it is only fair that we should know how much they cost the country. I am asking the minister if he will be kind enough to give us a chart of the Canadian Commercial Corporation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it has not been the policy of the government to disclose the salaries of employees of crown corporations engaged in commercial enterprises. Such corporations are working in a competitive field, and to disclose the salary of a first-class man is usually to invite competing firms to bid for his service and overbid the government corporation. This rule has been applied for years to Canadian National Railways with the endorsation of this House of Commons. Certainly in an enterprise such as the Polymer Corporation, which is in a highly competitive field, it would be unwise. Canadian Commercial Corporation has its own sources of revenue. The money paid to its employees is not voted by parliament but is earned through the activities of the corporation. For that reason I believe the usual practice should be followed, and the salaries of the employees not disclosed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am sorry to disagree with the minister. He cannot complain about my intentions, because some years ago I paid him the greatest tribute ever paid to anyone in the House of Commons. I have a personal admiration for him, because I know he is a man of action. But with regard to what he has said, the work done by the Canadian Commercial Corporation was previously handled by the Department of Public Works. The salaries of the various officials of the Department of Public Works are made known in the public accounts. If the work was done previously by civil servants of the Department of Public Works, whose salaries were made public, I do not see why the same thing could not be done now that we have another organization that is working in mystery. I am against that sort of mystery with regard to finance. It was the stand of my greatgrandfather, who voted for the ninety-two resolutions for the establishment of responsible government. The stand of my grandfather and of my father has been my stand,

that we should know how the money is spent which we are called upon to vote. There is no man so important that he should live in a cloud of mystery.
I shall tell the minister something else, and in a most friendly manner: it is the members of parliament who are responsible for what is done by these crown corporations. If any one of my constituents comes to me and asks how much the president, general manager, or anyone else in the Canadian Commercial Corporation receives, and I am not in a position to answer him, I shall be remiss in my duty. It is because I do not want to be remiss in my duty that I am insisting upon this information. I know the minister has his own views on the matter, but I shall tell him that he can be sure the men who work in the Canadian Commercial Corporation will no more leave their jobs than those who work in any other government department, and whose salaries are mentioned in the public accounts. I believe that is a fair statement, and I do not make it to embarrass the minister. I am merely expressing a deep personal belief, that we should know all about the expenses. This prevents abuses. How many crimes are committed in the darkness of the night? Few are committed in daylight. When parliament does not know the amount of an expenditure, there may be abuses. People will not know about it, and it was for that reason I asked for the reform of the public accounts. It took me about two years to get it from the then minister of finance, Mr. Ilsley, but some amounts were not mentioned in the public accounts at that time. I insisted on that information, and finally the then minister of finance said he would give it to me. My demand was supported by Mr. MacNicol and Tommy Church. I pay tribute to my friends who are no longer here, but we did a good job in having the public accounts straightened out.
I am not opposed to the government; I support the government. I tell the minister that it is time to stop these crown companies; it is time to have responsibility. If we read the act we find it is the minister who is responsible, and he is responsible to the House of Commons. But if the Canadian Commercial Corporation does something, who will know about it? If the Bank of Canada does something, we have a report that means nothing. I have nothing to add, because I have expressed myself clearly on the subject.

Will the minister explain how the provision works out in the event that he exercises his authority to demand the delivery of certain products? Unquestionably

these suppliers will have commitments to private concerns, and it is possible that these private concerns would be occasioned a loss in a transaction of that kind, where the minister stepped in. I suggest it is quite proper the minister should step in where defence supplies are concerned, but is any provision made to take care of these private customers if a loss is actually occasioned?

speechtext:

speechtext:
I should like to raise a point having to do with the power to requisition and compel delivery within a time and at a price that the minister specifies. You will notice that subparagraph (ii) of paragraph (f) of subsection 1 of section 3 provides that there may be a reference to the exchequer court with respect only to the matter of price, and that the court shall not have power to extend the period of time for delivery. That seems to me to be a very harsh provision. I can appreciate the feeling which probably lay behind the making of that provision; if power were given to appeal to the exchequer court as to the time within which deliveries must be made, then the delivery of some essential and vital material might be delayed pending the outcome of an appeal. Let us remember, however, that section 8 provides:
Every person who contravenes or fails to observe any provision of this act or of any regulation or order is guilty of an offence and is liable upon summary conviction or conviction upon indictment to a fine not exceeding $5,000.
It may be that the requirement made by the minister as to the time within which delivery must be made is unreasonable. Nevertheless in his view it is essential to secure the material. He issues an order for delivery within ten days, and it is next to a physical impossibility for the order to be complied with. Every effort may be made to comply with it, but it may be that the material is delivered not in ten days but in two weeks. That man has committed a contravention of an order made under this act and is liable to a fine of $5,000, but there can be no appeal to the exchequer court on the question of time. The only appeal is on the question of price.
It seems to me to be a most unwarranted provision to put in the act. The minister is taking sweeping powers. I do not propose to prolong the debate on that point, because we had it on second reading and the house decided yesterday by its vote that he should have these powers. The bill gives him sweeping powers, and it may be that they will be exercised arbitrarily in what the minister conceives to be the interest of the
Defence Supplies
country and in the interest of procuring the supplies quickly. I can quite see that that may happen. This man against whom an order for delivery within a time limit has been made finds that it is a physical impossibility for him to comply with the order, and he is guilty of a technical breach thereof and liable to a fine of $5,000. He cannot go to court and say that it was impossible for him to comply, because the exchequer court has no right to make any order or finding with respect to the time of delivery. I ask the minister if it would not be possible, without seriously interfering with his right to compel delivery within such time as he specifies, nevertheless to permit an appeal to the exchequer court to embrace the question of time, so that, delivery having been made, at least a man could defend his liability to a penalty by establishing in the exchequer court that the time specified by the minister was not reasonable under the circumstances.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, it is unfortunate, but the defence of a nation sometimes requires a government to be harsh. In England it is harsh to the extent of taking young men out of the normal walks of life and putting them in the army for a period of time. That has not been thought necessary in this country, for which I am very glad; but if the government had to be harsh and take material away from a man a little sooner than he would like to deliver it, that is just too bad, but it does not disturb me in the least. I have been administering this act for the last ten years, and I have not been harsh to an extent that has caused any great repercussions in the country. But we have been firm; if we needed something for defence we got it, and we got it when we needed it. That will continue to be the policy of the government, in spite of my hon. friend.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Let me make it quite clear,
Mr. Chairman. I said I accepted the fact that the minister held the view that he must have power to compel delivery. In spite of the insinuation the minister has attempted to convey, however, I am not objecting to the fact that it is necessary to insist upon deliveries. As the minister says, sometimes it is necessary to be harsh when the defence of the country is at stake. All right; he has taken power to compel delivery, but I say he should not go further and take away from the man against whom the order is made any right of recourse to the court in connection with the penalty he may incur because he has been physically unable to comply with the order. The order has been complied with as soon as possible, but not within the time limit laid down. The

Defence Supplies
difference may be only a few days, in spite of the best efforts of the man to make delivery on time. Nevertheless that will involve him in liability to a penalty of up to $5,000, and he has no right to appeal to the court on the question of time. I distinctly asked the minister if he did not think that, without cutting down his power to compel delivery, he could grant the subject the right to appeal to the exchequer court after delivery had been made, on this question of penalty, and that was all I said. I do not think it is necessary for the minister to insinuate that we are trying to make it impossible for him to obtain materials vitally needed for national defence. .

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, I am a layman, and my hon. friend is a lawyer, so I will ask him this. Does he know any way of collecting a penalty or a fine except through the courts?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext: No, I do not know of any way to collect a fine except through the courts, but the exchequer court is precluded from making any finding with respect to the time of delivery, whether or not the time fixed by the minister was reasonable. A man may exceed that time limit by one day; if he does, he is liable to a penalty of up to $5,000, and the exchequer court is specifically excluded by subparagraph (ii) of paragraph (f) from making any finding with respect to time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext: Then may I ask my hon. friend, as a lawyer, another question? How much of a fine does he think a court would assess against a man for being one day late in making delivery?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext: I do not care if it assesses a fine of only $1; the principle is there. The man may be two weeks late, but the court cannot go into the reasonableness or otherwise of the time limit; it is precluded from doing so.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend that it is their custom to do so.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext: Not when the statute specifically says the court may not make any finding with respect to time. I am quite sure the minister does not intend to suggest that the court would deliberately ignore the terms of the statute. However, I have made the point and raised the question, and apparently the minister thinks there is nothing to it. I have asked whether he did not think, without limiting his power to obtain delivery, he could nevertheless permit the subject to appeal to the court on the question of time with respect to the penalty he might otherwise incur.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext: I submit that in order to have a fine imposed a man must be brought into one of the courts of the land. The department makes out its case against him, and he presents his defence. I have never known a Canadian court to impose a fine when the person before the court had a reasonable defence, and I do not think my hon. friend has known of that either.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext: But there is no defence under the terms of this statute. His defence is taken away from him.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext:
This is the key section of the act, and it might make for more progress if we took it up clause by clause. I want to ask a question about section 3(l)(d), which reads:
. . . arrange for the performance of commercial and professional services.
That would seem to be a power which can be exercised in the normal course of business. Can the minister give us examples to indicate the necessity of having that provision written into the act?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, I am not suggesting that the machinery would not function without that section, but the desire is to make perfectly plain what are the powers of the minister in connection with procurement for the armed services. We wish to make it clear that it is within the power of the minister to obtain commercial or professional services if they should be required. Commercial services might be the storage of material. Professional services might be an independent opinion on a design problem, or various other services.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext: That means power to go out and hire somebody to do a special job; is that it?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext: That is it. The transportation of personnel would be a case in point.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Then in connection with paragraph (f) there is this provision:
. . . require any person who produces, deals in or has in his possession or control any materials or articles needed for the completion of a contract with respect to which a requirement under the authority of paragraph (e) has been issued, or needed for completion of defence supplies or a project being constructed or carried out by a government department, the Canadian Commercial Corporation or any company to which the Government Companies Operation Act applies . . .
That would appear to be a good deal wider than simply giving the Minister of Trade and Commerce power to carry out a defence project. Why is the provision worded in such a broad way? It says, "project being constructed or carried out by a government department," which might mean any one of the various government departments. Why is the terminology so broad?

Other agencies take part
in procurement. For example, Canadian Arsenals are a very important factor in procurement. Today Canadian Arsenals are making all the guns used by the army, and various other munitions; and the act should properly apply to them. If they find it impossible to carry on their work through lack of supplies, they should be able to requisition supplies through the minister. It applies to various crown companies accustomed to take part in the procurement of defence supplies. The Department of Mines and Technical Surveys has a part in it as well. It usually procures the minerals. In the last war they made certain optical instruments in a factory that was operated by that department. This clause is built to fit the machinery that was found to be necessary to carry out the defence procurement duties in the last war.

In clause (e) there is a provision that if the supplier of the goods does not agree to the price set by the minister, the dispute can be referred to the exchequer court. Under the Department of Munitions and Supply Act, as originally passed in 1939, disputes were settled by arbitration, which is the normal peacetime way of settling disputes of this kind. I suggest we should now go back to the arbitration method of settling the price, rather than put the person who has been compelled to supply these goods to the expense of fighting the case in the exchequer court. I believe this exchequer court provision was put into the Department of Munitions and Supply Act in 1940 or 1943, and I am confident that the result of that change was that very few, if any, people would go to the expense and trouble of going to the exchequer court. It seems unfair to put that burden on them. Why would it not be better to use the ordinary arbitration machinery?

It is not usual in government contracts of any kind to use arbitration machinery. The public works contracts do not provide for arbitration. The usual method of collecting a claim against the government is to refer it to the exchequer court.
I can say to my hon. friend that, so far as requisitioning is concerned, if any contractor has a case that will stand up in exchequer court, it is unlikely that he will find it necessary to go to the court to get proper compensation.

I do not think it is fair that in peacetime people should be put to that expense. Why not use the simple system of arbitration? The government is not going to be hurt very much by arbitration. It is certainly much more desirable from the point of
Defence Supplies
view of a person who has been forced to turn over those supplies. It is not a case of ordinary purchases, and there is no difficulty about such transactions. This section applies to a case where the minister has forced the person to supply the goods. It does seem that where drastic power of that sort has been exercised, the person against whom it has been used should be given every reasonable opportunity to have a fair price set by the simplest method. Going to the exchequer court is a complicated business, for example, for any firm in British Columbia. It may not be so difficult for a firm in Montreal, but for firms in the distant parts of the country an exchequer court action is an expensive procedure. I do suggest that the minister should give some consideration to substituting the arbitration procedure.
Mr. Chairman, if that were done it would mean instituting a new practice.
That power was given in the original Department of Munitions and Supply Act.

Yes, but we changed the act as soon as we realized how we were differing from ordinary government practice. It was changed in the first revision of the act. It would have established a new procedure for the administering of government contracts.

One of the
things for which we gave the minister credit was that he adopted a lot of new procedures. Speaking seriously for a moment, I think there is great force in what the member for Vancouver-Quadra has said. I put it to the minister that when he was in business the last thing he wanted to do was go before the exchequer court. That court is familiar with tax matters and things of that sort, but not with this subject. The sensible course would be that advocated by the member for Vancouver-Quadra. I see no reason why we have to follow slavishly the established practice and the minister has not done that; he has been a pioneer. I hope the minister will consider the suggestion, because I do know the same view is held by businessmen.
The minister made an answer, which he felt was a fair answer, to the member for Kamloops, about the conviction. The member asked whether anyone charged with dealing in goods would get a fair hearing in court. The basis upon which the member for Kamloops and I make that suggestion is the understanding that under the wording of section 3 (f) all the court will have to be told is that the minister said this was fair and reasonable, and the man did not carry

Defence Supplies
it out. Would it not be fair to let this section stand and ascertain from the Department of Justice whether or not that is their interpretation of it? If they take the minister's view, then this section will not be as bad as we thought; but if they do not take his view, then the ground is cut from under what the minister said. After a man got into court, the minister seemed to feel he should have a fair run for his money. We believe that is not the meaning of this paragraph (f).

The Minister of Justice has already passed on this act, just as he passes on every act that comes before the House of Commons. What does my hon. friend think is the meaning of the act? The crown carries no more weight before a court than the other party to the dispute. The court is there to see that there is equity as between the crown and the subject.
But that is cut down under the statute.

The court cannot do that when the statute itself says by implication that that defence is not open to the subject. Then the ordinary equitable jurisdiction, if you like, of the court is removed because it is bound by the terms of the statute.

Yes, but what is it bound to do? It is bound to impose a fine not exceeding $5,000. It can impose a fine of one cent technically, if the court thinks conditions warrant it. I may say that from the experience we have had in trying to enforce penalties under orders of this kind, that is about what the court usually does.

Paragraph (g) of this section states:
(g) require any person to furnish such information respecting defence supplies dealt in by him or projects of a type executed by him or respecting his production and other facilities relating thereto in such time and manner as the minister may specify.
It seems to me that this paragraph gives the minister power to require from any dealer in goods any information of any kind. Last week the Minister of National Defence told us that the army alone holds something like 170 million or 180 million pieces of equipment of one sort or another. The equipment required by the defence department covers practically every business which one can imagine existing in the country. It would seem to me that under those circumstances any business in the country could be required by the minister to furnish any information he wants to secure. Perhaps that is the intention of this section; I do not know. Will the minister tell us whether that is the intention of the section, and if not, what the intention is?
[Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood) .1

The intention is that all information that is needed in connection with defence preparations shall be obtainable. In other words, if the government wishes to make an inventory of any material to determine how much is held in the trade, it is their privilege to do so. If the government wishes to make an inventory of manufacturing capacity, as they did prior to the last war, it is the privilege of the government to require that information to be furnished by any firm. It is a reasonable provision, and a provision that is included in any defence act I have ever seen.
I take it the effect of that answer is that the section is designed to give the minister the power to secure any information he wants from any business in Canada.
That is right.

It seems to me that that is unnecessarily wide power to be given, particularly in view of the fact that when we come to subsection 2 we have there provision that this information can be given out and used under certain circumstances, and so forth; I shall have something to say about that later. But it does not appear to me that the thing should be as wide as it is. Paragraph (g) says "respecting defence supplies"; but when we come to the wording of it in connection with projects and other facilities that the people have, nothing is mentioned in connection with defence at all. It might be anything.

Does the section mean that the minister could send his representative into any business in Canada and get whatever information the minister wanted? As I read the section, it goes that far, regardless of whether that firm has anything whatever to do with the government of Canada. It may have no business dealings with them whatever, yet the minister can send a man in and demand any information that the minister sees fit to demand; in effect, that means any information that the officials of the Canadian Commercial Corporation see fit to demand.

That is
exactly it.

Furthermore, the section is wider than that because it applies to a project, and "project" is defined as covering a building, aerodrome, airport, dockyard, fortification, road or other work required for the purposes of defence. That means that the minister can send a man into any roadbuilding firm, any shipbuilding firm or any one of the construction firms; he can get particulars of the internal workings of any firm

which deals normally with projects of that kind, again regardless of whether or not that particular firm has had anything to do with any government.
The minister says that every country has provisions such as this. Yet Canada never had a provision of that kind until the war. There was never a provision of that kind in the Canadian law until 1939; and it was written into the Canadian law then because of the war and, as we thought, for war purposes. I think this clause is the most objectionable one in the whole bill. It is purely dictatorial, with no limitation on it whatever. I do not see how the minister can justify asking for such powers.

On section 3, subsection 1, paragraph (g).

In view of what the minister has said, and as I read this paragraph, it seems to me that it gives him power, for example, to send a man down to my farm to ask me how many pigs I am raising, how many I am figuring on raising in the next six months, how many cattle I have, how much grain I have, and so forth. He can ask me about any of those things. They are all necessary for defence. The defence forces eat a great deal of pork, beef, and so forth. It does not seem to me to be reasonable that the minister should have the power to send people into any business whatever in this country, and require the man running that business to answer any questions that may be put to him. It particularly does not sound reasonable to send these people out amongst the farmers. I do not suppose they would ever do that; nevertheless the power is there to do it, as I read the subsection. It seems to me that this provision should be amended to limit the powers to projects, let us say, which are specifically and necessarily used in defence preparations.

Will my hon. friend please tell me what clause in this bill allows the minister to count the pigs on his farm? Paragraph (g) reads:
require any person to furnish such information respecting defence supplies dealt in by him-

That includes pigs.
That is a defence supply?
You mention animals in one section.
Animals are considered now as defence supplies.
Ask the troops for their opinion.

No. I think the minister is all wrong about this, in spite of his legal opinions. Surely this would go quite far enough, especially when you read the extraordinary wording of paragraph (a) of clause 2 which says:
(a) "defence supplies" means arms, ammunition, implements of war, vehicles, mechanical and other equipment, watercraft, amphibious craft, aircraft, animals, goods, wares, merchandise, articles and materials of all kinds required for any project or otherwise for the purposes of defence.
I come back to this point under paragraph (g).
If my hon. friend will agree that we would not look into pigs until we call up pigs for defence, I think that we might agree. I think it means horses.

I am not
going to pursue the question of pigs. I really am more interested in something else. Under this provision it seems to me that the minister, and, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra said, a whole lot of other people who are acting for the minister, are entitled to go in and ask for information. Let us be realistic about this. Quite true, it is the minister's authority that is behind it; but actually there are a number of officials who are entitled to go in, I take it, to get all the information about patents and processes of any kind, things which may be very injurious. Again let me say that if this is all going to be done by the minister personally it might be-
Bad enough.

Well, bad enough, or good enough, but at any rate this is a very different thing. I think we have to be realistic about this. Surely (g) does do

exactly what the hon. member for Calgary East said. It opens the door wide, and it lets you get any information, secret or otherwise, confidential or otherwise.

My hon. friend would divide industry into two parts for defence purposes: those who are willing to co-operate with the government in giving information that the government requires to make a survey, and those who are not willing. As to those who are not willing he would say:	We will not
question those; they need have no part in defence; we cannot bother them; we will just deal with the willing ones, and the survey will represent what the willing people will say they can do in defence; with regard to the unwilling people, we will just count them out; they will not be a factor when there is a war. Well, when there was a war I do not recall that we made much distinction between willing people and unwilling people.

The minister says that when there was a war we made no distinction. We have said again and again, until I am sure the minister is tired of it and we are tired of saying it, but apparently it is necessary to keep on saying it, that the whole basis of our objection is that this is peacetime. What we are worried about is that these powers, these extraordinary powers are now apparently a commonplace in peacetime.

Unfortunately even in peace, for the defence of the country, some people think it is necessary to take harsh means. Now, if this represents harsh means, this country believes it is necessary to take this step.

I want to support what the hon. member for Calgary East has said. I take great exception to the last remarks of the minister, that we are dividing this country up into those who are willing to support the defence-
No, I did not say that; I said those willing to give information, and those unwilling to give it.

Those willing to give information and those unwilling. I can take the minister to many people who in the last war ruined their health in the performance of services for the country. Many of these people object today to this type of legislation being introduced by a government in peacetime. I tell the committee that they are very patriotic people. If there were another war, or if this country needed defence measures, these very same people who did so much that they ruined their health in producing food and so on, for the armed

services, would be willing to do it again. They do not think that we should have this type of legislation in peacetime.
I lost an opportunity to speak yesterday because I was called out of the house on something else. I cannot refer to that now, but I did vote against the bill. I would have liked to have an opportunity to speak on the bill, and speak on behalf of many people whose views I represent on this type of legislation in peacetime. It does not fit in at all with the day after day criticisms that we have made in trying to get information out of the Department of National Defence. It is in absolute opposition to anything that we have got from the Minister of National Defence. I want to say that that clause is something foreign to democracy as we have it in Canada.
Again to go back to many of our producers who are just as patriotic in the defence of this country as the minister or anybody else, they disapprove of this type of legislation. I cannot be too emphatic about that. I present the words "dividing up this country" which the minister put on the record a few moments ago.

I have said very little on this bill, 'but I believe that there is a fundamental change in the necessity of preparedness in peacetime from the conditions that existed many years ago. Years ago, as I have pointed out many times in the house, Canada had ample time after the outbreak of war to build up her material and equip and supply her troops. I have said time and time again that I believe those days have passed. It is necessary for us to take measures in order to prepare our forces for the defence of this country such as we have never had to take before.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Bring on the colonels.

We are very proud to have someone in our party who is independent and who does not always follow the party line. It does not worry us at all. I wish you had a few in your party.
To go back to (g); the minister has been kind enough to say he will have a look at (f). I want him to have a look at (g). I want to remind him of what he said a few moments ago, namely, that perhaps we do not need this legislation yet. I hope the people of Canada will come to know this. We talk about being harsh. What does harshness mean? It means, as the hon. member for Souris said, he assumes that there is a division, as he iddicated a few minutes ago, between the willing and the unwilling. I think that is an insult to the people who are considered unwilling. I say again that he
Defence Supplies
has not been able to give us a single instance to show that this power is needed, to show that there is anyone unwilling. I told him yesterday-and he ought to take this as a compliment-that he had very great prestige in the manufacturing community and that I believed he could do this without all these extraordinary powers. At any rate we now come to (g), and you have this inquisitorial power which, it seems to me, is foreign to everything. I wonder if all the men who voted for this so blithely yesterday read these things through, and whether they consider it is good. Are they prepared to have this inquisitorial power almost without limit?

I have not heard any suggestion from any member of the opposition of any practical amendment that could be made to this section. I have heard the appeal of a lawyer on a previous subsection. I have heard the opinion of a lawyer in the house, and I do not think there is any lawyer in this house or in Canada who could make an amendment to this paragraph which would be practicable in the working of the act.
The officials cannot walk in and make these inquisitions unless it has been directed by the minister that they make them. The minister himself is responsible to the public if he makes inquisitions. If they are unreasonable he will not be a minister very long. Therefore I say there is nothing we can do about this paragraph.
You have not been here very long; you do not know.

This paragraph makes possible the setting up of what might be called an industrial gestapo. It does not seem to me that it is necessary for the working of this act to have powers of that kind, power on the part of the minister to require all this information from any individual who is engaged in industry. It is completely against the liberties of the individual which we have always looked up to and protected in this country and which I think everyone in this country wants to have continued. This paragraph should be deleted or amended in such a way that the wide powers will not be there.

That is rather meaningless. There is no difference right now between us in our desire to see all the branches of our defence forces properly equipped and cared for. But this is peacetime. There is undoubtedly a right and a wrong way of doing this thing. We differ only as to the procedure. Why one minister should have all these dictatorial powers in peacetime I fail to understand. I am just as eager to see proper methods of defence in this country as anyone else. The present minister, who is now asking for these dictatorial powers, during the calendar year of 1949 insisted that the government should disregard and ignore the law of this land. At that time the Minister of Justice, who was sworn to observe and respect the law of the land, apparently lacked the courage to insist upon carrying out the law of the land or in turn to offer his resignation as any of his predecessors in that high office I think would have done.
Who wrote that one?

I wrote these notes
myself. If you know my writing you can check it and find out.
Read it if you like.

I feel keenly about this matter. I was referring to the Combines Investigation Act and the flour milling report. I know something about conditions in this country. Surely the Minister of National Defence should have some responsibility in the matters covered by this present measure. He and other cabinet ministers are dodging their responsibilities.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I must remind the hon. gentleman that we are dealing with paragraph (g)-
Under which great and wide powers are given to the minister.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: -which deals with information which the minister can ask to be furnished.

I was referring to what the same minister has done in the past calendar year, and now we are being asked to give the same minister much wider powers. As I pointed out before one o'clock, some people with whom I am personally acquainted are just as patriotic as any others and care just as much about the defence of this

country. They disapprove of this legislation. I think there is a greater feeling about national defence in this country at this time than there was at any time in previous history. During the last great war there were differences of opinion in this country; there were those who believed, with the best of intentions, that no troops should leave our shores. They felt that our energies should be confined to production. I am not criticizing their view, but there was that division. Today it is realized that if there is another war this country may be the Belgium of that war. The result is that there is a much more united feeling about matters of national defence. Irrespective of what we think about its being a privilege to serve in the armed forces, there is no lack of concern in any corner of this house about national defence or a desire to see that all members of our armed services are properly equipped and cared for in every respect.
It is an entirely different thing to give one minister all these powers, especially those provided for in this paragraph (g). I know it has been said that this is being made a personal matter, but I contend that no minister should be given that power. It should be a matter for the cabinet to decide and surely the Minister of National Defence should have responsibility in these particular matters.
As I have pointed out before, we have spent days discussing the estimates of the Minister of National Defence, and so far we have not succeeded in getting anything that would lead us to believe that there is a need for legislation such as this in peacetime. There certainly is no argument about the desire of any of my colleagues to grant authority in the proper way. I have pointed out that there is a united feeling about national defence in this country, but there are many people who are just as patriotic as anyone in this house who disapprove of this legislation being passed in peacetime.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: What about the hon. member for Nanaimo?

The hon. member for Coast-Capilano asks, "What about the hon. member for Nanaimo?" I made it very clear at the start that there is no member in this House of Commons for whom I have more respect than that hon. member. I pointed out that there was no difference between us about national defence and the providing of proper equipment and care for our troops. It was probably only a matter of the detailed methods about which there might be some difference. I respect the hon. member because he has had much more experience than I have had.

I will go further. I have been pointing out that the Minister of National Defence should have some concern about this. The other day the hon. member for Mackenzie made some remark about colonels and so on and said that he and the Minister of National Defence had served as buck privates. I would remind him that some of those colonels were originally buck privates. I do not think it can be said to be against them that they became colonels after serving as buck privates. I know that some of those colonels refused promotion for some time, men who have debated this matter in this house.
What are you discussing?

I am discussing national defence. Has my hon. friend any objection? It may even be that some of the brass hats would rather have a buck private as Minister of National Defence than a certain major general to whom reference has just been made. We have freedom of thought.
I repeat that we have objection to any one man being given the powers granted by this bill.	.
Section 3, subsection 1, paragraph (g) agreed to.
On section 3, subsection 1, paragraph (h).

Paragraph (h) deals with the construction and repair of ships. It gives the minister power to specify, subject to the approval of the governor in council, to what shipyard this business will be sent. As I read the paragraph it covers more than ships for the Department of National Defence; it would include shipbuilding for any department of the government. That would seem to be an unnecessary addition to the Defence Supplies Act. I ask the minister whether it would not be ample for the purposes of the act to have the power limited to ships to be constructed or repaired for the Department of National Defence.

The purpose of the paragraph is to divide government ship contracts of all kinds among shipyards in an equitable manner so that we may be able to keep in operation the shipyards that we believe we would require in war. During the last war our shipyards were expanded tremendously. If contracts for ships were let on the basis of tender, as required under the Public Works Act, you would have a situation where dog eats dog, and in my humble opinion you would only have three shipyards left in operation. You would have one on the west coast, one on the St. Lawrence and one on the east coast, and the others would be bankrupt. I think that is inevitable because
Defence Supplies
the yard that is best able to get the initial business and keep its overhead low is bound to get any following business. In the interests of national defence I think it is not desirable to see our major operating shipyards reduced in number from eleven to three. For that reason, on the advice of the Canadian maritime commission-and I must say anything the department does in connection with the allocation of shipyard work is done on the advice of the maritime commission-we are taking the power in the act to allocate not only work required by the naval services of national defence but also any departmental work that a department may wish to have allocated. I remind hon. members that we allocate nothing unless we are asked to do so by the department directly involved. We can allocate on requisition from a department of government. Some departments will probably prefer to call for tenders as they must do under the Public Works Act. If other departments can be persuaded by the Canadian maritime commission that it is desirable to allocate their work, and they wish to make a requisition on the Department of Trade and Commerce to undertake the allocation, then this paragraph in the bill gives the department the power to do just that.
Has the minister any power to allocate the construction of new shipping without approval of the governor in council?
No.
The section is not quite clear whether the power to act without the approval of the cabinet is limited to the repair of ships as distinct from the construction of new ships.

It is limited to urgent repairs the estimated cost of which is not more than $50,000. The only emergency power the minister has concerns an urgent repair, or in any event a repair not costing more than $50,000. Otherwise allocation can only be made by the governor in council.
What is the objection to keeping the figure at $5,000 as set out in the Public Works Act?

The objection is that a boat may run aground, and commitments may have to be made exceeding $5,000 before it can be hauled off the reef. It is thought that $50,000 will likely cover emergent salvage operations, and therefore the figure is placed at that amount.

As I read the section, the ceiling of $50,000 also applies where the repair is not of an emergent nature; to ordinary repairs as to which time is not of such

Defence Supplies
importance. Is it the intention that all ship repair contracts under $50,000 should be allotted by the minister without the approval of cabinet, or is that power supposed to be restricted to emergency repairs?
What does the bill say? It says, is urgently required.

It says, "is urgently needed or does not involve an estimated expenditure", and so on. It may be that the word "or" should be "and". It makes a great difference in the coverage. What was the original intention?
I imagine that the people who drafted the bill intended it to be as it is, "or".
Then the way the bill reads it covers both cases. Any work up to $50,000, even though it is not of an urgent nature, can be allocated by the minister without the approval of the cabinet.
Yes.

Mr. Chairman, I agree that the questions put by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra at the present time are perfectly in order, but I want to make a necessary distinction about secrets. There will be secrets about matters concerning strategy and no secrets concerning expenditures. When we heard the leader of the opposition speaking so much about strategy I presume he was voicing the views of the Tories of the general staff of the Department of National Defence, and to that I am opposed. There shall be no discussion of strategy in the House of Commons, but a full discussion of expenditure. I hope the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra will tell that to his leader when he returns to the house from attending the meeting of the standing committee on public accounts.
Section 3, subsection 1, paragraph (h) agreed to.
On section 3, subsection 1, paragraph (i).

This paragraph gives the minister power to employ the Canadian Commercial Corporation, or any company to which the Government Companies Operation Act applies, to exercise under his direction such of his powers under this act, other than those under paragraphs (e), (f) and (g), as he may specify. What other corporations has the'minister in mind as likely to be used for the purposes of this act? Why does he not include in the powers which cannot be assumed by the corporation the power as to shipping? It seems to me that paragraph (h) should be added to paragraphs (e), (f) and (g) as one where the minister himself should be responsible.

The minister is responsible for the operation of every clause in the act. He has the power to delegate except for the three clauses mentioned. In other words, if it is a case of demanding priority the minister authorizes that personally. No other signature is good. If it is a case of requisitioning it must be the minister's signature. If it is a case of applying for information it must be the minister's signature. As to the allocation of ships upon the advice of the Canadian maritime commission, there is no reason why that power should not be delegated. It is a routine power. The minister has the responsibility for it just as in the case of all other clauses, but it is a power that he can very well delegate.
What about my first question concerning other government corporations?

As to other government corporations, Canadian Arsenals is the principal one. It is handling about $40 million worth of business today, which is delegated to it by the minister. The Polymer Corporation might very well be called upon to assist in stockpiling rubber. Any crown company that can do a job more efficiently than a government agency may be called on for that purpose.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has just referred to the Canadian Commercial Corporation and the maritime commission. I challenge him to denounce the Tories who are in those crown companies.
The hon. member for Temis-couata is full of challenges today. I do not know whether he is looking for a fight or trying to be funny.
I am not trying to be funny; I am very serious.

I did not know there were so many Tories in Canada as he has mentioned today. I am glad to learn that we have such extensive support, and I hope we can find more. I am trying to do business with the Minister of Trade and Commerce at the moment.

On section 3, subsection 1, paragraph (j).

This paragraph provides that the minister may-
-do such further things as may be authorized by the governor in council in regard to the procurement and disposal of defence supplies and projects.
I would like a little information as to why the word "disposal" is in here. So far everything has been in connection with procuring supplies for defence purposes, but

apparently this paragraph gives the minister power, when authorized by the governor in council, to dispose of any supplies or projects. I thought the normal way that was done was through the War Assets Corporation, that these supplies were automatically turned over to them for disposal. Is it proposed to have some different procedure with respect to the disposal of surplus defence supplies and projects, or what is the reason for this provision?

Occasionally the department gets a requirement from another government for certain supplies. The need may be urgent, in which case, after it has been cleared by the Department of External Affairs, reference is made to the armed services to see whether they would prefer that we deliver existing stocks to the customer and replace those stores with new material. In some cases the answer has been in the affirmative. My hon. friend will appreciate that ammunition particularly is subject to deterioration and very often the army prefers to deliver ammunition from existing stocks and have it replaced in due course with fresh stock. In that case sales are made; the money is put in escrow and used to pay for the replacement of the store through Canadian Arsenals.

From what the minister has said I take it that the word "disposal" is put in here so that this provision will be complementary to the paragraph in the National Defence Act which was passed last week and which provided that with the authorization of the governor in council, articles which were not surplus could be disposed of; and it was explained at that time that it was to permit them to be disposed of to foreign powers. I take it the only reason for including the word "disposal" in this paragraph is that materials may be turned over to other powers, and that the ordinary means of disposal will be followed otherwise.

That is a correct statement.

On section 3, subsection 1, paragraph (f).

Being a layman, and not being very clear as to just what was my hon.

friend's point, I asked the Minister of Justice to attend. If my hon. friend will state his point now I have no doubt the Minister of Justice will be glad to deal with it.

I appreciate that. If the Minister of Justice will have regard to the terms of section 8 as to the imposition of a fine; then if he will have regard to the terms of section 3 (1) (f), he will see these words:
-who having received an offer that, in the opinion of the minister, is fair and reasonable, has refused delivery of such needed materials or articles, to deliver them-
In the first place, when queried as to section 8, the minister said under that section a man would get just as fair a trial as he would get in any other legal proceeding, but the view was put forward that actually the court would be restricted by the terms of section 3(1) (f) because the determination there was the opinion of the minister, and anyone indicted under section 8 would come before the court having refused to do what the minister said and would be faced with paragraph (f), which, as I see it, makes the opinion of the minister conclusive on the court.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Conclusive as to what; as to
the time for delivery?

As to the reasonableness of
the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Subparagraph (ii) contains
these words:
-such reference-
That is, to the exchequer court as to price. -shall not extend the period of time for delivery specified by the minister under subparagraph (i).
Is that your point? From a cursory reading of this section I would say that what it had in mind was that the minister would specify the time and price. If the price were unacceptable it would be settled under paragraph (f) (ii) by the Exchequer Court of Canada, which would determine the current market price. Then if there were an alleged breach of this section which was required to be prosecuted under section 8 I should think the court-which incidentally would be an altogether different court than the Exchequer Court of Canada, since such a prosecution would be carried on in the ordinary criminal courts-upon considering the charge that the accused to comply with the reguisition which would be able to consider whether there was a reasonable opportunity on the part of the accused to comply with the requisition which the minister had made. Take an extreme case, in which the time specified by the minister was perfectly satisfactory and reasonable, and still was not complied with. If

Defence Supplies
the accused could come along and show that he had been hit by a car at the time he was preparing to comply with this request, and so had a good and reasonable excuse for not having done so; it seems to me that that would constitute a good defence. This is not like the adulteration acts, for example, where a man selling some kind of food product has no means of knowing whether or not it is adulterated because it is only handled by him in the ordinary commercial way. Yet it is necessary to impose upon him an absolute, outright obligation that the product be pure, and if it is not, he is guilty whether or not he has any guilty mind. From a casual reading of this statute now before us, I should think it would be necessary for the crown to prove mens rea. Then, if the crown were able to establish a prima facie case, the accused could come along and show that there was an absence of mens rea by proving the facts of his defence.

I have no
desire to prolong this discussion, but I want to make the point perfectly clear. I am going to read some particular lines to the minister and ask whether in his opinion it is open to the court to review the decision of the minister in this connection. If the Minister of Justice will look at lines 16, 17, and 18, he will see that they refer to a person having received an offer that is, in the opinion of the minister, fair and reasonable, and has refused delivery. My question is, will it be competent to the court to review the decision of the minister, and reach its own conclusion as to whether the order is fair and reasonable?

May I just follow that up before the minister replies? Surely that is the main point, those words in lines 17 and 18 to which reference has been made by the member for Greenwood. They must be read in the light of the subsequent provision that the exchequer court is precluded from taking into consideration or making any finding with respect to the time at which delivery was to be made. The whole implication of this paragraph is that the minister has the absolute right to set the time, or first to make an offer which includes both the price and the time of delivery. If the person to whom the offer is made fails or refuses to deliver, then the minister has the right to make an order compelling him to deliver. Under the words of the section read as a whole there is, by necessary implication, an absolute right conferred upon the minister to make a decision as to time, and the words "fair and reasonable" are part of that right. Any requirement which he makes as to time, therefore, must be considered as being fair by the court when interpreting the statute by virtue of the

provisions in the statute. I believe it is open to serious question whether the court can go behind the words of the statute and make its own inquiry, or indeed receive evidence on the question of whether the time limitation fixed was fair and reasonable.
It should be borne in mind at this point we are not asking that the exchequer court be allowed to prolong the time within which delivery may be made so as to defer delivery. That is the point the minister does not want to allow. We are referring to the proceedings in the ordinary court into which a man may be haled for the imposition of a penalty, in spite of having done his best and having failed to comply with the terms of the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, is not the point this, that offences generally, as I indicated a few moments ago, for the purpose of the present discussion are divided into two groups. There are those offences, and I think this covers the great majority, in which it is necessary to prove mens rea as an ingredient of the offence, or that the accused had, in relation to the alleged offence, a guilty mind, an intent to commit a breach of the law. Then there are offences, and I believe this constitutes the minority of offences, such as those relating to the adulteration of food. In the public interest it has been necessary to dispense with any proof of mens rea in such cases, for it is necessary that you find a man guilty who is selling an adulterated product, regardless of the fact he may have had no knowledge whatever that that product was adulterated.
I cannot find anything in the present statute, just in a casual perusal or upon hearing the point raised by my hon. friend the member for Greenwood, to indicate that the offence which is created here falls into the second category. If it does not fall into the second category, then it would be necessary for the crown to prove mens rea, that in relation to this matter the accused did have a guilty mind. Let us say that my colleague, in a manner which would certainly not be characteristic of him, made a demand which was absolutely unreasonable as regards time for delivery-that his demand could not possibly be complied with. I certainly cannot imagine any court, upon the accused being brought before it, under section 8, that would ever refuse to receive the evidence which the accused would adduce to show that this demand was unreasonable, and that the accused could not comply with it.

Will the
minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

I repeat that I am not going to drag this out, but I wish the minister would read again the words of section 8, which is to the effect that every person who contravenes or fails to observe this act is guilty of an offence. Is the minister still prepared to say that this section only contemplates an offence where there is a guilty mind?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, I think so, because if my hon. friend will look at almost every section in the Criminal Code, or the Official Secrets Act which we sought to amend today, he will see this phrase repeated time and time again: Every person who contravenes this section shall be guilty of an indictable offence, or an offence punishable upon summary conviction. The point I am making is that it is not spelled out in the section of the statute which creates this sort of offence that it imports the idea of mens rea. Yet the idea of mens rea is there, and if the accused can show, in relation to any statutory offence, which does not fall within the second category of offences, that in point of fact he did not have a guilty mind to commit a breach of the act, then that is a good defence.

I believe there is probably a weakness in this section which has not been noticed. Apparently the offence would be a refusal to deliver, and that would be a direct act. It does not say that if a man does not deliver he is guilty of an offence, it says if he refuses to deliver then he is guilty. I believe, so far as the minister is concerned, that he has a weakness in the act which he has not recognized. In other words there has to be a refusal to deliver, not a failure to deliver within a certain time, or he cannot be guilty of an offence.

speechtext: He would start with the police court.

Carried.

On section 3, subsection 2-Non-disclosure of information.

In view of the last remarks, I hesitate to raise another point, but I must say that I am more impressed with the argument of the Minister of Justice in this case than I was with the argument of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, although by that I do not intend to detract from his knowledge of the rules of this house, for which I have the greatest respect. The point I wish to raise here is a question with regard to paragraph (c) of subsection 2 which it seems to me again gives to the minister the right to disclose information or rather to make available information gathered under paragraph (g) of subsection 1; it seems to me to give the minister the right to disclose that information in any civil action or proceedings, without any limitation being imposed on that right. Again it may be argued that obviously this right will never be used in an unfair or prejudicial manner; but I would ask the Minister of Justice, since he is here, if I am not correct in my opinion that there is no limitation, as the result of the working of this clause, on the right of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to disclose the information which he has acquired, in any action whatsoever, or proceedings whether or not they relate directly to the operation of this act or whether they arise out of any contracts or negotiations entered into under this act. In other words the minister, with the broad words that are in this paragraph (c) of subsection 2, has the right to disclose that information in any proceedings whatsoever. Subsection (2) reads as follows:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:

No person shall' disclose any information-
Without the consent of the minister. That will refer to any official in the minister's department.
