speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I have a few remarks I should like to make and I also intend to move an amendment.
A legal amendment?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Yes. It is perfectly in order. There are two subsections in this section. Subsection 1 repeals the Department of Munitions and Supply Act with the proviso that certain sections of that act will continue to apply to certain contracts specified in the subsection. One can have no quarrel with the repeal of the Department of Munitions and Supply Act for it is being replaced by the powers set out in the bill now before us.
Subsection 2 repeals the Defence Purchases, Profits Control, and Financing Act, 1939, and thus wipes off the statute books the only bit of legislation which places a limitation upon the profits to be made out of defence and

Defence Supplies
war supplies. I realize that section 7 of the Defence Purchases, Profits Control, and Financing Act, 1939, which placed a limitation on the profits, was overridden by the Department of Munitions and Supply Act, but under subsection 1 of this section that act goes by the board. Without getting into too much of a legal argument, it seems to me that if section 7 of the Defence Purchases, Profits Control, and Financing Act of 1939 remained on the statute books, it would now apply. My point, if I may state it again, is that the statute that overrode the 1939 act is repealed by the provisions of subsection 1 of section 9 of this bill. That leaves the 1939 act alive, at least for the time being. I for one feel that section 7 of the Defence Purchases, Profits Control, and Financing Act, 1939, should not be wiped off the statute books.
Keference has been made during the course of this debate to some of the things that were said when that act was brought before this parliament during the first session of 1939. The late Ian Mackenzie, who was then minister of national defence, introduced the measure and made many references to the feeling in the country that profiteering in war supplies was abhorrent to the people of Canada and something to which the government wanted to put a stop. At page 1767 of Hansard for March 10, 1939, the late Ian Mackenzie said:
The government, if I may speak for them, believe in the principle of equality of sacrifice; that in wartime men should not be required to offer their lives and limbs while those who provide the weapons of destruction have even the possibility of reaping undue profits.
He also said on the same occasion:
The government is determined that in peacetime, where private industry must be utilized, there shall be the strictest possible regulation of profits both in the interest of the taxpayer and in deference to public abhorrence of profits made from products which involve destruction of human lives and misery among nations.
I would remind hon. members of the quotations the hon. member for Kootenay West made yesterday from articles written in years gone by by the present leader of the opposition. I would also remind members of the quotation that the leader of the opposition gave us yesterday from a speech made by Mr. Mackenzie King in years gone by. We are all together; we all say the same thing, that we do not want profits to be made out of the manufacture of war materials.
The particular formula or provision set out in section 7 of the Defence Purchases, Profits Control, and Financing Act, 1939, may not be the best way to achieve the aim of limiting the profits to be made out of war materials,

but until something better is produced I for one do not like to see that formula and the principle behind it wiped off the statute books of the country. As I have already said, it is the only take-the-profit-out-of-war provision on our statute books. I have heard the explanations made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce on a number of occasions as to why the government found it necessary to override the provisions of section 7 of that act in the fall of 1939. Maybe the explanations are acceptable and maybe they are not, but whether they are acceptable explanations or otherwise it seems to me that the mere statement that one particular formula was not satisfactory is not a sufficient reason for doing away altogether with the principle of taking the profit out of war. I would go further and say that I think 5 per cent is too much profit to be made out of producing war materials; I think all profit should be taken out of war, and then perhaps we might get rid of war itself; but at least we have that kind of provision on the statute books now, and I do not think we should take the retrograde step of doing away with it.
I believe the course that parliament should follow at this time is to retain that provision on the statute books. Then if the government feels that that particular formula is not the best one for doing the job let them bring in an amendment to provide another formula. In the meantime let us not wipe out the only piece of take-the-profit-out-of-war legislation that we have. I am sure that that provision is the least that the Canadian people want. I may say to the government that the Canadian people have not forgotten the fact that the 5 per cent clause was overriden in 1939 by the Department of Munitions and Supply Act. I know there was a good deal of feeling about it. I know that if the committee makes the decision now that that legislation is to go by the board for good, many Canadians will wonder just what it is all about.
The surest way to give Canadians confidence that our defence policy is clearly a defence policy, and that we have not yielded to the greed involved in profits made out of war supplies that was mentioned by the former prime minister, Mackenzie King, the leader of the opposition and others, is for the committee to say today that we are going to keep section 7 on the statute books at least until something better is provided. Toward that end, Mr. Chairman, I move:
That clause 9, subclause 2, be amended by adding thereto immediately after the word "repealed" the following words:
"except for section 7 of the said act, the provisions of which shall apply to all contracts made under this act."

So that it will be clear on Hansard what the effect of the amendment will be, may I say two things. First of all I should like to read section 9, subsection 2, as it would read with my amendment. It is as follows:
9. (2) The Defence Purchases, Profits Control, and Financing Act, 1939, chapter 42 of the statutes of 1939 (first session), is repealed, except for section 7 of the said act, the provisions of which shall apply to all contracts made under this act.
The other thing I should like to do is to indicate briefly what is contained in section 7 of the Defence Purchases, Profits Control, and Financing Act, 1939. It is a rather lengthy section with nine subsections and one of the subsections has three subparagraphs. But the gist of the section is contained in the first two subsections, which I should like to read. They are as follows:
7. (1) The maximum net profit received by any person in respect of any contract to which this section applies shall be limited to an amount equal to five per centum per annum on the average amount of capital of such person employed in the performance of the contract.
(2) There shall be levied upon and paid to His Majesty, by any person who is a party to a contract to which this section applies, a tax equal to the amount by which the net profit in respect of any such contract exceeds an amount equal to five per centum per annum of the average amount of the capital of such person employed in the performance of the contract.
As I have already indicated, there are seven more subsections, making nine in all. The others give details as to how the principle of this section is to be applied. I should like to point out that if my amendment carries it would then make the provisions of section 7 of the Defence Purchases, Profits Control, and Financing Act, 1939, apply to contracts made under the bill now before us, which is known as the Defence Supplies Act. I feel very strongly that we should not wipe out section 7. The remainder of the Defence Purchases, Profits Control, and Financing Act, 1939, can go. Those provisions have been replaced by other provisions, but until something better is produced section 7-the only take-the-profit-out-of-war legislation we have-really ought to stay on the statute books of Canada. I hope that the committee will support my amendment.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I can shorten the discussion by pointing out the objections. It has been found in practice that the clause in question is entirely unworkable. For example, milk is one of the supplies bought in large quantities. How would my hon. friend determine the capital employed in producing milk? I suppose it would be the value of the cow. Under that clause the government would be limited to paying a price for its milk that would return
Defence Supplies
5 per cent per annum on the cost of the cow. You can multiply that example by any number, but the one I am giving obviously meets the situation. There are a great many. The worst is where the production is a very small fraction of the output of a certain industrial plant, and it is quite impossible to determine the amount of capital employed in the production of the article in question.
I might point out also that I believe when that act was passed the tax on corporate profits was 5 per cent. Today it is 38 per cent in all provinces except Ontario and Quebec, where it is 40 per cent. Suggest for example the profit margin be written down from 5 per cent to 3 per cent. If the total profit a man may make is 3 per cent of his capital, he would be much better off buying dominion government bonds, which yield about that, and sitting back collecting his 3 per cent without producing anything at all. That would be the course of prudence, because in that way he could not lose. My hon. friend is not making any provision to take care of losses; he is just eliminating profits. If a man is interested in profits, the kind of man my hon. friend is trying to curb, he would certainly find a sure way of getting profits and of avoiding losses. I just mention these things to show how utterly unworkable that provision is; therefore it is quite unacceptable to the government.

speechtext:
If I may just have a word before the leader of the opposition rises, as the minister probably knows, in the latter part of section 7 there is an exception respecting contracts for which there is competitive bidding or tendering, whatever the phrase may be; I did not take time to read the whole section to the committee. The other comment I make is that I am not now asking the committee to accept something I have devised. which the minister, in presenting it, said was really the best that had been done in the field of limiting profits on war materials.
And it never worked.
It was never tried.

This is the last section of the bill. It is not necessary to review the discussion that has taken place, but before this section is carried I do think it appropriate to examine what really is happening through the repeal of the two acts mentioned in this section and their replacement by this single act. Nevertheless I recognize the point made by the minister, and there may be practical reasons why a fixed limit is not satisfactory to cover the over-all field. The statement has been made already that the Canadian Commercial Corporation is able to perform these duties and that it has been regarded as the agency to purchase in the place of the department of munitions and supply, and to carry out the functions related to the munitions and supply act. On March 24, 1949, when an amendment to the Canadian Commercial Corporation Act was before the house and

the minister was speaking in support of that amendment, he had this to say at page 1946 of Hansard for that year:
It was set up that way at first, but since it has become the purchasing agency for the Department of National Defence, since it has taken the place of the Department of Munitions and Supply, if this amendment passes it will be a continuing agency.

On one point I do not think there is any real difference of opinion in this house. Therefore, whatever expression is made on this section at the present time, one can do no more than to place on the record views which conceivably may have some influence on the operation of this act. I am speaking now to this amendment which is, in itself, not complete, but in raising it for the purpose of discussion I think it has served the purpose. Once again it brings before us the fact that we are doing away with an act that was introduced by this government, and hailed by this government as a progressive piece of legislation to avoid any abuse in connection with the production of defence equipment. In addition to the provision for the reasonable limitation of profits, there were other safeguards such as the calling for tenders. Those safeguards now disappear. I think this is a retrograde step, and in addition I do not believe we have been given any sound reason for the introduction of this legislation in this form.

I want to get my own mind clear on this subject. The measure before the house now not only repeals the Department of Munitions and Supply Act, but if section 9 of the bill passes it repeals the Defence Purchases, Profits Control and Financing Act which contained a provision for the limitation of profits. Unless we are prepared to amend section 9 of this bill as suggested by the member for Winnipeg North Centre, then we are not only wiping out the Department of Munitions and Supply Act but we are also wiping out the Defence Purchases, Profits Control and Financing Act. That is one thing we want to understand. This one measure is replacing two that had some merit.
With regard to the argument of the minister that the limitation on profits was not carried out because, as set out in that act, the formula was not workable, it is my honest opinion that the formula was not tried out. I cannot see any reason why it was not workable. In trying to let contracts at that time the minister might have done his best, but I do not believe that the people with whom he was dealing accepted their responsibility during wartime. I believe that the events which transpired in the latter part of the war with regard to plant and equipment bear out that

Defence Supplies
statement. The minister says it would be difficult to work out a formula to get the capital invested in any given project. I do not believe he was serious when he made his comparison with the cow. I may be simple-minded, but simple-minded people are honest, and I believe that anyone with an honest approach could work out a formula. There would be little difficulty about it.
In the event of an emergency the minister might want a munitions plant put up, or he might want the Canada Car and Foundry to extend its peacetime plant to build aeroplanes. I do not think there is ay difficulty in determining the cost. All the Canada Car and Foundry has to do is to allocate a certain portion of its plant to build aeroplanes and retool it. The only capital invested in the particular project is the cost of stripping the plant of its peacetime machinery, and retooling to go into the production of aeroplanes; that is the capital investment. Then, of course, there is the cost of constructing the aeroplane. There is no difficulty if you decide the profit limitation under a war contract is going to be 5 or 10 per cent. If the person who is going to manufacture war materials is interested in the war, is interested in the principles you are fighting for and in the maintenance of your institutions-democracy, freedom and all those things-he should not worry too much about making a whole lot of money. I do not think that those who manufactured war materials tried very hard to apply that formula when you consider that the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who was minister of munitions and supply at that time, said that they did their best but that they could not let any war contracts with that profits limitation provision in them.
I am also not unmindful of the statement that was made by Right Hon. Arthur Meighen who was in the Senate during the time that this controversy was fairly hot. He said that hundreds of his business associates-and this statement may be found in Senate Hansard- were resting on their oars because there were not any profits to be made; and if there were no profits in war, there was nothing to fight for. That is the actual quotation as I remember it. The hundreds of those business associates were not trying very hard, on the basis of patriotism, to work out that formula of limiting profits on war contracts.
As one member of this committee who has listened to these discussions a good many times, I do not accept the suggestion that that formula of limiting profits is not workable.
I think it is easy to work. I do not say whether you should draw the line at 5 per cent, 10 per cent or 20 per cent; that is
[Mr. Gillis.l
immaterial. But before we close this discussion I think that we should at least retain in that defence purchases act the principle of profit limitation in the event of an emergency. If we do not accept the amendment now before the committee, we are not only wiping out the Department of Munitions and Supply Act but we are also wiping out the defence purchases act. This act is one of the statutes passed in 1939, and it contains that principle. Despite the fact that it has been there since 1939, it was overridden by the Department of Munitions and Supply Act. No attention was paid to it and millions and millions of dollars of the money of the Canadian taxpayers were spent in building during the war, plant and equipment which was written off at accelerated depreciation. It was not a matter of making profits during the war but it was a matter of getting millions of dollars' worth of plant and equipment that was written off in three years under that accelerated depreciation plan. Nobody suffered.
I think we should benefit by the experience we had just a couple of years ago, and that every one of us should seriously consider not throwing the whole responsibility on one minister. This particular matter is one for every member of the committee. It is not a government matter at all. It is a matter of principle. I am seriously suggesting that we should understand what that amendment proposes to do. It merely proposes to retain in the defence purchases act the principle of profit limitation. If and when it is necessary to fight a war, and I hope it will never happen, then at least you have the principle there; and in the event of an emergency, someone has authority, under the terms of the act, to sit down and work out some kind of formula with regard to the limitation of profits.

Mr. Chairman, this is the resolution which is presented each year to introduce a bill to provide for the financing of the Canadian National Railways. Each year the Minister of Transport presents
Canadian National Railways to parliament the annual report of the Canadian National Railways and the budget for the coming year, which is then referred to the sessional committee on railways and shipping, owned, operated and controlled by the government. That was done this year on March 23. The committee had 22 meetings, and presented its final report to this house on May 11, at which time they had adopted the budget of the Canadian National Railways and the Trans-Canada Air Lines for the coming year.
The Minister of Transport then turns to the Minister of Finance to introduce a finance bill to provide for the capital expenditures which are included in this budget. This present resolution is identical in terms with the resolutions of previous years with the exception of the actual amounts involved and the deadline. It actually falls in three parts: First of all, the authorizing of the Canadian National Railways to issue securities, in this case not exceeding $24,582,489 in principal.
The second part is that the government is empowered, on the security of these securities, to make advances to the railway against its capital expenditures until such time as it is judged opportune to float a bond issue.
The third part authorizes the government to make advances to the Canadian National system in case their current revenues are not sufficient to cover current operating expenses and income charges. It is here that the only change in this resolution occurs. Always before the deadline for such advances has been March 31 of the year ahead. Last year, for example, the resolution had the deadline March 31, 1950. However, the lateness of the presentation of the report this year has got us in this position, that we are now past that deadline. Since March 31 the government has had no authority to make such advances to the railway, and as this will probably happen again it was thought best to advance this deadline to July 1, 1951. I expect that to be carried on in future years, so that the parliament will have passed this bill and the authority for such advances thus made before the July 1 deadline.
I do not think there is anything else that I can say here. I have here a great mass of detail on the bill which I suppose may best be discussed when the actual bill is before the committee.

Mr. Chairman, immigration is so closely linked with all forms of civil, economic, social and religious activity in this country, it has such far-reaching effects on the present and future life of this nation, that the solution of this problem affects our whole social structure.
The working classes are most concerned with immigration such as it is practised by the present government. It worries them a great deal, since it provides dangerous competition. The workingman is fully cognizant of the fact that the unscrupulous employer may thus find a pool of cheap labour into which he may dip at will, and which will allow him freely to regulate his employees' wages and, consequently, their standard of living.
Whether we like it or not, and with all due deference to my honourable friends, may I be permitted to say that immigration is and will remain a source of unemployment in Canada, as long as we are not in a position to take more active care of the newcomers, as long as the opportunities for farm settlement in Canada remain limited.
However, it is not my intention to deal with this very complicated question in all its implications and from all angles, but I simply want to make known the views of my constituents on this matter.
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) recalled in his budget speech on March 28 last:
Total labour income, in spite of the one per cent fall in employment, has continued to increase, and its monthly rate at the end of the year was about five per cent above the same months a year earlier. Average weekly wages rose about three per cent during the year, while the cost of living advanced barely one per cent.
While the decline in employment as a whole has been small, the increase in unemployment has been greater, due, of course, to the fact that the total labour force continues to grow. The outlook for 1950 seems to be that the volume of employment will increase moderately, but it is possible that it may not catch up with growth in total labour supply.
These words, besides indicating unequivocally that the problem of an ever-increasing labour supply is disturbing the politicians who, during the last war, promised that there would be no unemployment after the war, clearly indicate that industry this year will be unable to cope adequately with the demand of those seeking employment to allow them to secure the necessities of life and, especially, to face 'the high cost of living.
If unemployment was anticipated-in fact, the government did not believe in it since this evil had befallen us long before the minister made in the house the statement to which I have already referred-why then persist in bringing to this country immigrants who are apt to glut an already overstocked labour market?
The position of the Canadian economy is such that it cannot absorb such mass immigration as we have had since 1945. On the contrary, present circumstances would seem to call for a complete halt in immigration until jobs have been found for all our own people.
During 1949 the civilian labour force of Canada, including Newfoundland, averaged approximately 5,200,000, a gain through natural increase and net immigration of 110,000 over 1948. Employment averaged 5,055,000, an increase of 80,000 over 1948. Unemployment, defined as those wholly unemployed and looking for work, averaged 145,000 in 1949, an increase of 30,000 over the previous year.
Those statistics, taken from the budget papers, show that in spite of the vastness of our territory, the extraordinary wealth of our resources, the rapid expansion and constant progress achieved by our country during the past fifty years, excessive immigration is disrupting our economy. Commenting upon those facts, Le Devoir wrote as follows on April 30 last:
If unemployment is on the increase, it is not because our economic activity is decreasing, but rather because the number of jobs does not increase

Supply

Citizenship and Immigration as rapidly as the number of workers. This can be demonstrated mathematically. During the year, the number of workers increased by 110,000, while the number of jobs available increased by only 80,000. There is a difference of 30,000. Thus, there are exactly 30,000 more unemployed. The equation is perfect.
Unfortunately, the white paper does not distinguish between the contingent of new workers supplied by the normal increase in population and the net contingent afforded by immigration. Possibly, the shortage of 30,000 is about equal to the number of workers who have migrated here. In round figures, some 360,000 immigrants have come to Canada from the time the war came to a stop to the end of 1949. As the percentage of workers was high among these immigrants, they must have numbered over 200,000. And we had 145,000 jobless.
Now, in mid-June, hundreds of thousands of workers are still unemployed.
In my constituency alone, the latest reports indicate that a few thousand people are still looking for work, but to no avail.
What will happen next winter when insurance benefits are exhausted?
On the other hand, we are told that so far the government has favoured a selective immigration policy. I should like to know in what way it has been selective.
Did the government try to bring into Canada immigrants of Anglo-Saxon origin only or Jews expelled from every country in Europe? How has the government chosen between English, French, German or Spanish immigrants? Has any preference been shown for any one race, language or creed? If so, for which race, language or creed, and why?
Did the selection apply only to moral, health and political standards? I don't know. But I do know that miners, domestic servants, labourers were brought in, as well as a great many people who are neither technicians nor experts and who, consequently, are likely to be unemployed at the first sign of a recession.
If we need highly skilled craftsmen, scientists, men of learning, it is not only a good thing, but a desirable and necessary one to facilitate their coming to this country. But Canada must not be considered by other countries as the natural outlet for their surplus population. Canada should not be made a ghetto or a back-door to the United States.
An editorial on this subject, which appeared in the April 4th issue of Le Soleil, the Liberal party's official paper in Quebec, makes interesting reading. It is entitled "Against mass immigration." The writer says:

One of the natural consequences of the neighbourly relations between Canada and the United States is that a great many earnest workers are prevailed upon to leave the poorer country and move to the wealthier and more favoured one, in the hope of bettering their lot. That unfortunate situation has arisen everywhere borders are easily crossed. This loss of the very blood and sinews of this country has had its effects on every class, even among refugees and immigrants. In spite of these losses, our population is increasing, as well as employment opportunities, but in unequal ratio.
And it is surprising to learn that unemployment is also growing when employed workers are more numerous than ever. In view of these circumstances, for what practical purposes does the government still want to admit thousands of foreigners for whom there is no need generally in the professions, in industry and in business? The only reasonable explanation for this policy is that, first, the country will need more mouths to use up our agricultural production and more hands to defend our shores in case of an invasion. A reason less readily admitted is the device of using D.P.'s as return cargoes on our otherwise empty ships. Before these newcomers are able to bring returns to the nation which extends hospitality to them, they are dependent on the poor as on the rich, on private charity as on public relief, on large families already overcrowded in small accommodations as on the owners of magnificent residences. And each immigrant finding employment takes a potential job away from the student or the apprentice seeking to settle in his own native country.
We, the people of Chicoutimi county, want to keep Canada for Canadians. The pioneers of this country have indefeasible rights, of which our government is not free to deprive them for the benefit of certain promoters of immigration. Instead of spending millions to bring over from Europe fur merchants, ladies' wear manufacturers and dealers in ready-made garments, we should think of our wage earners, of the humble folk, of all those of our people who falter under the heavy burden of taxes and the high cost of living, and use a few of those millions to alleviate their distress and suffering, as well as to provide jobs for them.

Mr. Chairman, it would be difficult for the member for Rosedale to remain silent in this debate upon the estimates of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. The population content of the riding is such that it is important that I place before members of the committee certain views on the important question of immigration. We have in Toronto-Rosedale unity in the midst of diversity from the standpoint of the various racial groups in the community. We have the usual groups which are found in the majority

throughout Canada. I refer to those of English, Irish, Scotch and French origin. They are in the majority in the riding but we have several important racial groups in the riding constituting a strong body of new Canadians. They are proud of their traditions and the great things that make them what they are.
I should like to mention the Hebrews, Macedonians, Poles, Ukrainians and Italians in particular. They are citizens who are proud to be Canadians. Right within the riding of Rosedale they demonstrate a spirit of tolerance second to none in Canada, and they live in harmony as true Canadians beside their fellow Canadians of the majority group. Despite diverse racial origins and creeds there is great harmony and a spirit of community building amongst us. This is genuine democracy and true Canadianism.
I may say I was much impressed with the speech made the other evening by the hon. member for Vegreville. He demonstrated to the house the fine motives which actuate these new Canadians in coming to make homes in our land. These new Canadians are very grateful to the minister for the sympathetic consideration he has given to their submissions placed before him from time to time. Nevertheless, like all people who desire new immigrants for this country, they do not receive all they seek from time to time, and they have thoughts they wish put forward in the house as to how the immigration laws of Canada can be improved.
Naturally the problem of immigration brings forward extreme points of view. I was not in the house when the hon. member for Spadina made his speech, but from reading Hansard I gather he made a rather sweeping indictment of the government on the subject of its immigration policy generally. From reading that speech it seems to me the hon. member for Spadina was saying that the government had no policy or, in the alternative, that what policy it had was an echo of oft-repeated principles devoid of substance.
With this view I cannot agree. I go back to the policy of the government as stated by the former prime minister; and I say that policy, enunciated in May, 1947, in my opinion remains the soundest policy for Canada. Let us examine it as I summarize it under three heads. The first point of the policy was and is that the government does not seek to alter the fundamental ethnic character of Canada. Right-thinking Canadians agree with this, and I believe the majority of the people throughout Canada approve this principle. The second point of the policy is that immigration shall be related
3G75
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration to the absorptive capacity of Canada. Whc will disagree with this fundamental point, which I believe has the approval of our people generally? The final major point of the immigration policy of our government is that there shall be selection of immigrants with care, to the end that those we bring here to share our freedom and our political institutions shall be loyal to the spirit of freedom and to those institutions in Canada.
Having in mind this policy, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me the day for mass immigration has gone, if ever there was one. Those words "mass immigration" form an ominous phrase with an ominous connotation. Visualize, if you will, hundreds of thousands of immigrants coming to our country from the four corners of the earth. They descend upon our cities, towns and villages. Let us assume they are unprepared for gainful employment and absorption into the life of Canada; they may even be unfamiliar with our skills. If they come in too great numbers we can be sure they will have no practical means of livelihood in Canada. Care must be exercised. Is it any wonder, then, that organized labour has placed on record its view that there shall not be mass immigration into Canada but that in effect there should be selective immigration. We do not want to undermine the labour unions. We do not want to bring such a great number of immigrants to this country that their labour may be used as a means of depressing wages. Immigrants are brought to this country to build Canada and bring new skills, to the end that there may be production of new wealth. Let us take this view of immigration and we will be on sound ground. Let us stimulate the production of consumer goods; we will have nothing to fear if our immigration policy is designed toward this end.
The policy I have stated has been applied to a preferred group in a very careful manner. We have given preference to those of English, Irish, Scottish, French and American origin; and I do not think anyone in this committee would quarrel with that preference. After all it is the people of the British isles to whom we owe the great ideas of government which prevail in this parliamentary democracy. The French explored the great rivers and vast spaces of this land in the beginning, and in one province we have their civil law. The United States has always been a great factor in the economic life of this country, and we welcome people from that country if they choose to come here. We do not labour this point, because it is obvious.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
On the other hand there has been a more restricted outlook as to the people of other countries; but I do not blame the government because within the last few years immigration has fallen off. Other factors have been responsible for this, and over these factors the government has had no control. I mention that in western Europe an export ban has been in effect on capital, which has had much to do with the falling off of immigration into Canada. I say, too, that we must not blame the government for refusing to go headlong into some over-expanded program of subsidies for transportation costs, loans against frozen assets and other financial assistance to aid immigration. I take it the departmental officials have kept in mind that about twenty years ago we had what was known as the British empire settlement scheme. Mark you, I am not an expert, but from what I am told that scheme was not so successful as to invite repetition in this year of 1950.
I do not criticize the policy of the government, but I say that its application can be extended at this time, and in that connection I have a few suggestions to put forward. Let us have more immigration agreements with countries abroad. Through such agreements we can regulate gainful employment here for the immigrants who may come, and we can seek some financial assistance from the countries abroad. An example of this is the Dutch agricultural scheme, which has worked very well in bringing Dutch farmers to Canada. Is it not possible for us to implement agreements of this kind with countries such as Great Britain, Ireland, Scotland, France, Switzerland and, let us say, the Scandinavian countries? Perhaps we cannot negotiate such an agreement with the United States, but by other means we can stimulate immigration from that country if we go about it in the logical way.
In the end, therefore, those countries not mentioned in my remarks up to this point remain to be considered. What are we going to do there? Many of them are behind the iron curtain, and in those cases immigration becomes very difficult. Many of them have displaced citizens in those countries of western Europe I have mentioned. In my view we must look to the regulations. Let us consider, and let the minister through his officials consider, the abolition of what I call rigid, artificial, inflexible rules. There is the country of origin rule, which in effect blocks out whole groups of worthy immigrants. There is the degree of relationship rule; many people are not near enough in degree of relationship to those who sponsor them. Can we not do something about altering this rule? Let me sum it up in this way. Let us


judge the value of each immigration application on its merits, through some administrative tribunal within the department, and let us have an honest evaluation of the merits without artificial regulations hindering immigration.
Finally I wish to say a word about what I call selection. That is important to all of us, because we know that the matter of security is paramount to Canadians. We do not want to bring immigrants here to build up the economic side, if they be the wrong type from the standpoint of security and undermine us on the political side. We have to allow for human error, and human error will prevail to a certain extent. Let us, Mr. Chairman, make our regulations in such a way that there will be security screening, just as strictly as possible, from the standpoint of keeping communists from immigrating to Canada.
I speak with confidence as I stand here today to conclude my remarks. My confidence is all the greater because of the minister who occupies the post of citizenship and immigration. He is known to us as a lawyer, as well as a soldier of distinction. It was a personal loss to the Prime Minister when he placed him in this post so important to the government of the day. As parliamentary assistant to the Prime Minister he served with distinction, and we know that his talents will be well employed in this important field. Just as he served before the bar of international public opinion, he will serve at home and solve these problems which we are considering. May I say to him that, as he is a great Liberal, let him liberalize these immigration regulations in accordance with his personal qualifications. The result will be a good one, I think; immigration with justice and moderation.

Mr. Chairman, I think it is
significant that so far in the discussion of the estimates of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, practically every speech made has dealt with the subject of immigration rather than the other matters falling under the jurisdiction of the same department. It seems to me that indicates there is the greatest concern on the part of the members of the house, as well as throughout the country generally, about this important subject. That is not to say that the others are less important, but it is difficult to imagine any subject where there is more potential good for the country than in a properly applied and vigorously pursued policy of immigration.
It is also significant to note that, although there have been two or three statements from the government side of the house, practically every speech made has been, to a greater

or less degree, critical of the policy of the government, and more particularly of the application of that policy. While I should like to say that I agree with the member for Rosedale in the soundness of those parts of his remarks applying to the necessity for maintaining adequate security precautions in connection with our immigration, in connection with not disturbing the ethnic balance of our present distribution of population, I cannot agree with him that the application and pursuit of the policy of immigration by the government has been so successful as to deserve any commendation whatever. I join rather with those who, while realizing the difficulty of this problem, nevertheless feel that the steps taken so far are disappointing, and that this house should leave no doubt in the mind of the government during the discussion of these estimates that it feels we have been sadly lacking and must do better in the future.
In studying this question of immigration, it is quite significant to find that there are comparatively few books or papers or treatises on the subject of immigration as a whole, particularly as applied to Canada. I should like to bring to the attention of the members of the committee one of the few available reports or studies. It is a study instituted in the province of Saskatchewan in 1930, and the findings are contained in the report of the Saskatchewan royal commission on immigration and settlement presented to the government of Saskatchewan in 1930. I am not going to devote any time to a lengthy analysis of its recommendations, but I should like to lay before this committee some of the considerations discussed in that report, as well as some general considerations which I propose to make the basis of a motion I intend to bring before this committee.
One of the first recommendations made, and which seems to me has application at the present time, is that any scheme of immigration must be worked out in conjunction with the provinces because it is to the various provinces of this country that the immigrants will go. It is under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments, and through close contact with the people in the welfare fields, that the new settlers will be raised. I think that no time should be lost in convening a group to study that problem alone. I do not believe it is sufficient to say we are having a dominion-provincial conference this fall. I believe that conference is to be concerned with entirely different matters. It is essential that a conference should be convened to study this matter; and, to start with, a meeting of the departmental officials of the various governments who would be concerned should be" held. There should be a meeting of the
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration officials from the provincial departments of lands . and resources with their opposite numbers in the federal government, to work out at the official level a basis for a joint program or a joint submission to the joint governments for an immigration scheme.
Then other considerations follow with respect to the importance of immigration generally, and the reason why we must set about bringing into Canada a substantial number of immigrants. The various considerations laid out in the study to which I have referred are still of the most urgent and practical application, even though the report was made twenty years ago. Certain other considerations have arisen' since. One of the most compelling is the need of national defence. An area which is as large as or larger than the continental United States, an area which would undoubtedly be the prize possession of any other country, is not capable of being defended by a nation of only thirteen million or fourteen million people. While we are fortunate in being assisted in defence schemes by the United States of America, and in being able to rely upon them to assist us in the joint defence of the North American continent, I do not believe any hon. member will think we can escape our responsibility for the defence of this part of the North American continent, this Canada of ours. I doubt if any hon. member would disagree with me if I were to say that in the world of today, Canada almost certainly cannot herself defend her territory. It would be shirking our responsibility if we failed to face the fact that, without a substantial increase in our population, we will not be able to discharge our primary responsibility in that regard.
Then there is the consideration concerning the importance of one of the principles found in population studies over the years, population and economic studies, to the effect that it is necessary for the population of a country to reach a certain level numerically in order for the country to be able to maintain its high standard of living. It must be admitted that, so far as my study went and so far as the report of this commission went, there are no figures available for Canada. Nobody has yet worked out the actual optimum population level for this country. But I feel again that no hon. member will disagree with me when I say that it is certainly questionable-in fact, I think it is almost impossible-to expect that we should continue much longer to be able to sustain the standard of living which we now enjoy, and which we properly expect, with a population of only thirteen million people and with budgets at the present time running at a level of two and a half billion dollars and quite conceivably growing to three billion dollars in the immediate future, particularly as
3G78

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration defence requirements and social security and similar commitments grow, as the government undertakes further responsibilities.
With a static or virtually static population of only thirteen million people, with the tremendous problems which this country imposes on us with respect to communication, with respect to the development of resources, by its very area and the very size and difficulty of the terrain, it is almost impossible to expect that, in a world of increasing standards and of increasing requirements, we should be able to maintain the present standard of living let alone raise it, unless we increase our population and therefore considerably expand our productive capacity.
Then also there is the question of the loss of population which occurs through the economic attraction of other areas. It has been alleged in the past, and I think it has been established-although the figures vary-that we suffer a substantial loss of population from year to year by the attraction of the generally higher standards of income enjoyed in the United States. Hence, in considering the question of increase in population, we have to reckon not only with the fact that, by the normal increase involved in our excess of births over deaths, not only would our increase be slow on that account, but the increase itself is made less speedy by the fact that we lose each year a certain number to the United States.
In considering this and other factors, the Saskatchewan commission came to a conclusion which I think is sufficiently important to be read in its own original words at this point. As reported at page 18, they said:
For these reasons we conclude that it is desirable that no unnecessary checks be placed on population increase by immigration.
They go on to deal with the fact that certain checks are necessary, but they come back to their original contention that no unnecessary checks should be placed on population increase by immigration.
I should now like to turn to one other aspect of this matter, and that is our particular relationship with Great Britain and with the British commonwealth. I have said that I agree with the hon. member for Rosedale that it is important that the ethnic balance of population in Canada be not disturbed or distorted by any over-enthusiastic policy of immigration. Our traditional connection with the United Kingdom, together with the present situation of the United Kingdom, seemed to me to indicate that we should make a special effort to obtain suitable immigrants from that country. I shall have something to say in a moment about the necessity of obtaining immigrants from

other countries, a matter which I think is equally important, but I wish to deal specially with the question of British immigration.
I believe that one should approach this matter without a limited horizon. One should remember what has taken place over the last couple of hundred years in connection with the concept of the British commonwealth and the relations that those countries bear one to another. One should remember that Great Britain has not only exported standards of living and sent people to every part of the world, but has also exported the great idea embodied in what we call British justice and the rule of law. Then it seems to me that we should devote at least some thought and some part of our ideas and aspirations towards preserving that concept and preserving a continuity of that relationship. But no country and no group of countries can stand in the face of history or of development. History is that the centre of influence, the centre of population, or the centre of power shifts. I believe that fact has to be accepted and realized by all countries in the British commonwealth if we are to maintain intact, and to preserve from undue stresses and strains, that friendly relationship which we have had in the past.
I should like to see that relationship as close as or closer than it has ever been. My concept is of no change in our affection for or attitude towards one another but simply a recognition of, and acceptance of, and indeed an assistance to, the course of history in shifting the centre of the British commonwealth from the United Kingdom to the various member nations of that commonwealth.
I believe that Canada's resources, potentialities and political maturity all have such an important bearing on this matter that, viewed in their proper light, we can without exaggerating look forward confidently to the day when we shall be the centre of the commonwealth, the centre of a tremendous group of world powers. That involves a readiness on our part to accept, and admittedly a readiness on the part of the United Kingdom to permit, a considerable flow of emigration from the British isles to this country.
I think that perhaps it would be well if we could have with the British authorities that consultation which the hon. member for Rose-dale referred to, from that point of view, and say: Do not stand in the way of history; do not place impediments in the way of free movements of people as you are doing now by restricting the people from the United Kingdom in their coming over here; do not

place those impediments in the way of the free movement of people because, if you do, you are standing in the way of history.
I do not want to overdevelop this thought. What I have in mind is this. Surely it is no longer logical for us and for other countries to continue to export raw materials and food over thousands of miles to places where they may be manufactured and re-exported back here. Surely it is much more logical, and surely it is the proper course of history and development, to see that people come to where the raw materials and the food are, bringing with them their industrial knowhow, and the same traditions and ideals which we share and which, in fact, have inspired the growth of the commonwealth. The movement of population from the United Kingdom to Canada, under that concept, would be part of a logical, natural process; part of the growth and the preservation of that commonwealth which we value so much. But just as we say to the United Kingdom, you must not place impediments in the way of the free movement of people, so must we also be prepared to encourage and to assist in the movement of people from the United Kingdom and other countries to this country. I cannot be satisfied that we have made every effort to assist in British immigration. I myself have letters, I have discussed the matter with other members and with other individuals in Canada who have spoken to people with similar experiences; that is, experiences of difficulties when they applied to Canadian authorities in the United Kingdom, difficulties placed in their way, or at least a lack of all-out enthusiasm, help and assistance in ironing out the difficulties which stand in the way of those people coming into this country. I believe that Canada could do much more to assist immigrants from the United Kingdom. I believe that Canada must do much more to assist that immigration.
Before I leave this general idea that I have been dealing with may I say I think it significant that this Department of Citizenship and Immigration follows almost immediately the estimates of the Department of Agriculture. In the last day and a half of the discussion of that department we were dealing with the difficulty of marketing Canada's tremendous agricultural production. I have said already it seems illogical to ship our raw materials and raw food thousands of miles, have them manufactured, and then shipped back again. How much more logical it would be to have the people come to where the food and raw materials are. That should be one of the conscious thoughts behind the

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration immigration policy; that the long range solution of our agricultural problems-while we may adopt floor prices, support programs and programs of encouraging or discouraging this or that aspect of agricultural production, which are necessary so long as we have such an imbalance in our economy-rests upon bringing more people to this country to consume the food that we produce.
I have found, too, that very few studies are made of the number of people that would be necessary to produce a balance in our economy in that respect. But I did hear one very eminent authority discussing this matter, Dean demerit of the department of agriculture of the university of British Columbia, who has since retired, say that his estimate was that if we would bring to Canada, or if our population were increased by, five million people we would have a practically balanced economy, from the point of view of there being sufficient people in Canada to consume the things which we produce with the exception of one crop, namely, wheat. With respect to apples, pork, beef, and almost every other agricultural commodity that you could name, with the exception of wheat, it was this expert's calculation that an increase in our population of five million would practically solve that problem of the imbalance, of our dependence upon the export market.
These, Mr. Chairman, have been pretty general considerations on a general subject on which, as a matter of fact, there is general agreement, namely, the necessity for a conscious and an active immigration policy in so far as this country is concerned.
What I want to turn to is some of the shortcomings in our policy. I regret very much that what I have to say should be said at a time when a new minister is occupying the position of Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, because no member of the house, be he a new member or one with the longest experience here, cares to make a sharp criticism of a new minister. Therefore I ask the minister if he will-and I am sure he will-regard this simply as a criticism of government policy and in no way arising simply because he is new to the office.
He will get it next year.

The figures with which I have been furnished indicate a very disturbing and sharp decline in the flow of immigrants to this country over the past two and a half years. We all thought, after the Prime Minister made his statement on government policy on May 1, 1947, that we could expect to see, if not in the year, at least within the

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration next year and the year after a constant and steady increase in the flow of immigration until finally it reached quite sizeable proportions. These expectations have not been realized. We remember the interest-and I think I would not be going too far if I said the enthusiasm-with which the statement of May 1, 1947, was received. I well remember the headlines in the press across this country, hailing this great new immigration policy, as it was called.
My main criticism of it is that while the principles laid down are sound enough, not only have they not been applied, not only have no positive steps been taken to apply the principles, indeed nothing was said at the time to indicate how they would be applied, and nothing has happened since to indicate that there is any serious intention of applying them and of bringing in the large, increased and increasing number of immigrants which was then forecast.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Before six o'clock I was outlining some of the general considerations which should apply to any immigration program we might adopt and indicated the necessity of taking active steps to increase Canada's population by immigration. I should like to turn now to some of the shortcomings in government policy and particularly to the failure of the government to take steps to implement the immigration policy which it has laid down. It is convenient at this time to refer to a statement made by the Prime Minister on May 1, 1947, and which gave rise to such hopes that we would in fact have an immigration policy for Canada productive of results. These hopes have totally failed to materialize. The Prime Minister is reported on page 2644 of Hansard of May 1, 1947, as having said:
The policy of the government is to foster the growth of the population of Canada by the encouragement of immigration. The government will seek by legislation, regulation, and vigorous administration, to ensure the careful selection and permanent settlement of such numbers of immigrants as can advantageously be absorbed in our national economy.
The figures on immigration which we have obtained since that time indicate that the policy has failed totally of implementation. I do not recall any legislation that has been introduced which is of far-reaching moment in regard to this matter. With regard to regulation, it was pointed out by one of the members of the government party speaking

this afternoon that the main effect of the regulations seems to be to restrict rather than to encourage immigration. With regard to vigorous administration, figures which I shall quote in a moment show that the main effect has been that while the inflow of immigrants has declined by some fifty per cent, the cost of administration has increased by some twenty-five per cent.
The Prime Minister then went on to outline the short-term program and the longterm program of the government. The shortterm program was related to the situation as of May 1, 1947, when, as he pointed out, we were confronted with a serious shortage of shipping and, therefore, it would not be possible to bring large numbers of immigrants to Canada. But with respect to the government's so-called long-term program the Prime Minister laid down basic principles which are to be 'found on page 2645 of Hansard as follows:
Let me now speak of the government's long-term program. It is based on the conviction that Canada needs population. The government is strongly of the view that our immigration policy should be devised in a positive sense, with the definite objective, as I have already stated, of enlarging the population of the country. This it will seek to attain through the development and energetic application of productive immigration measures.
Then a few sentences later on:
Apart from all else, in a world of shrinking distances and international insecurity, we cannot ignore the danger that lies in a small population attempting to hold so great a heritage as ours.
Before I give the actual figures of our present immigration I should like to refer to a speech made in Ottawa on Saturday, May 27 last, by the present minister. Remember that we have a country with a larger land area than the continental United States and with a population of only 14 million people. At one time this country absorbed between 500,000 and 1 million people a year. There were certain disadvantages that accrued during that heavy inflow of population but I submit that their causes have largely disappeared with our reaching a relatively high degree of * development in the present populated areas of Canada and with our high degree of industrialization.
Speaking in this city on Saturday, May 27, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration said that in the view of the authorities at the moment Canada would be capable of absorbing a population which on a certain mathematical calculation turns out to be 140,000 a year by way of immigration. I submit that that is much too low a target for our immigration policy under the circumstances in which we find ourselves. Yet that is the only indication we have had as to what the

government thinks should be absorbed and even that target, if it be a target, is far in excess of the number that are being brought in today.
I have spoken already of the desirability of a large flow of immigration from the British isles, and I should like to refer to some of the other countries from which we should receive immigrants. At the present time the inflow of immigrants from continental Europe is seriously restricted by the regulations. I know that one cannot go too far in relaxing regulations against those who were our enemies five years ago, but I maintain that the interpretation of the regulations is far too restrictive, and so is the classification of enemy aliens.
We all know that there has been a tremendous upheaval on the continent of Europe. People whose only offence is that they happened to live in countries which were overrun by the nazis and were caught up in that turmoil and swept into Germany or into countries which had been overrun by Germany are now classified as enemy aliens, and are now excluded, except those who are in a very limited category with regard to relationship to Canadian residents. In many cases they are the relatives of people who are most admirable citizens, people who came here with very little and who have built up a livelihood for themselves and a stake in this country, people who are now prosperous and substantial citizens in the best sense of that word. Yet their relatives are prohibited by the regulations from coming in at the present time. This is a matter on which positive action by the government is required to relax those restrictions and allow these desirable settlers to enter the country.
What is the government going to do to encourage immigration from the United Kingdom? As far as one can make out, virtually nothing has been done up to the present. We are told that the currency restrictions stand in the way. What we need is a bold approach to this matter. The government should be prepared to adopt means by which we could offer to prospective immigrants from the United Kingdom an extension of currency privileges in this country based upon the security of assets guaranteed by the United Kingdom government. Without something along these lines, so long as the artificial restriction of currency barriers continues we will prevent people from coming here because they cannot get the funds out to this country from the British isles. I ask the minister to tell us what discussions have taken place on that point, what is the intention of the government in that regard,
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration and what representations or offers they have put forward to the British government in that respect.
Finally I want to come to the question of the figures of present-day immigration. [DOT] In answer to a question which I asked, information was given, as recorded at page 1902 of Hansard, that the average monthly number of immigrants entering Canada from Europe, including the United Kingdom, for the calendar year 1948 was 9,352. In 1949 it was 6,966, and in the first three months of this year it has fallen to 4,823. So that our flow of immigration from the continent of Europe, including the United Kingdom, has fallen by 50 per cent since 1948. If you look at the estimates, Mr. Chairman, you will find that during the same period the cost of the domestic administration of the Immigration Act has risen by 25 per cent. For the year 1948-49 the domestic cost was $3,403,000; for 1949-50, $4,191,000; and for 1950-51, $4,482,000, an increase of $1,079,000, or 25 per cent during the period in which our intake of immigrants was falling by 50 per cent.
That is the outcome of the government statement which was so widely hailed on May 1, 1947, that we were to embark upon a policy of fostering immigration by legislation, regulation and vigorous administration. The only result is a 50 per cent decline in the intake and a 25 per cent increase in the domestic cost. It is true, and no doubt the minister will point out, that the cost of overseas administration has declined. I suggest that if we are going to have a policy of immigration, overseas is the very place where we should be spending more money in order to assist immigrants to establish their nationality and to assist them to solve their transportation and currency difficulties. That is one place where an increase in expenditure would be justified, but I submit that an increase in expenditure as to domestic costs is entirely unjustified during a period when our intake from overseas has been declining by 50 per cent.
I am quite sure you will agree with me when I say that I have probably detained the committee long enough, but in view of the matters which I have laid before the chamber, and particularly the facts to which I have just referred, I think I am justified in moving a motion by way of censure. I am not saying that when we get to the details there will not be other matters which could be attacked and where specific reductions might be moved. We do not in any way bind our hands in respect to their reduction, but at

Mr. Chairman, I intend to speak only briefly on this subject. When speaking before six o'clock the hon. member for Rosedale referred to the factors which govern the immigration policy, and he urged


that the basis be broadened. The hon. member for Kamloops also referred to the need for encouragement of an increase in British immigration. With both these arguments I am in complete accord.
What I should like to refer to is a rather narrow feature of the whole matter. In so doing I should like to deal with a few of the factors mentioned by the hon. member for Rosedale. He referred, for instance, to health as being a governing factor, and said that there could be no quarrel with the government for insisting that all immigrants have good health. Of course that is a matter for the medical services to determine. He also, mentioned absorptive capacity. I might mention as an illustration the workers brought in a few years ago for the pulp and paper industry. Rural members from Ontario, Manitoba and other western points will recall that some years ago sufficient workmen could not be found for the lumber camps. Recruiting went on to get every farmer's son- who could be spared -for that work, and at the same time a drive developed to bring in displaced persons as immigrants for work in the woods. Now, within the last year or so, our absorptive capacity for these immigrants has been reached, and there has been no further need for a policy which would encourage the immigration of workers for the lumber camps and pulp and paper mills.
I propose to deal briefly now with a very narrow phase of immigration which would not conflict with either of the two factors I have singled out. I want to suggest one kind of immigration which I believe has been greatly neglected; that is, immigrants to go into domestic service in this country. I would not care where those people might be recruited from, whether it be Great Britain, France, Holland, Belgium, Denmark, Germany, Italy or any other suitable European country; I am sure all hon. members will agree that there is a great shortage of domestic servants in this country. That being so, no one could object to their entry on the ground that our absorptive capacity was not great enough to take care of them. They are needed badly. I know that figures are rather dull, but in this connection I want to quote a few. At page 3029 of Hansard answers were given to questions I had placed on the order paper as to the number of displaced persons brought to Canada in 1947, 1948, 1949 and up to April of 1950. These figures indicate that
10,000	displaced persons came to Canada in that period of time and accepted employment as domestic servants for at least a year. The answer to my next question, on the same page, shows that the number employed in domestic service has dwindled rapidly from 1931 down to the present time. According to

this answer, the number of people so employed in 1931 was 146,000. By June 1, 1948, that figure had dropped to almost half, or 74,000. About that time there was a slight increase, which I believe could be largely explained by an answer given to another question I asked having to do with the percentage of the population employed in domestic service. In 1931 that figure was 1-4 per cent. By 1947 it had fallen to 0-4 per cent, but the following year there was an increase to 0-6 per cent. In other words if we take the 7,200 displaced persons who came to Canada in 1947 and 1948 and undertook domestic service for a period of one year, I believe it would be fair to assume that the small increase of 0-2 per cent could be attributed almost entirely to that immigration. On that basis it would take about 28,000 domestics to make up the percentage deficiency today as compared with 1931.
I do not suggest that my argument is airtight, nevertheless I think in the main it is sound. So I suggest that the. department give some consideration to the decrease in the number of domestic servants in Canada, and the possibility of making up that deficiency through immigration. I heartily agree with what the hon. member for Kamloops said about British immigration, but I doubt very much whether our domestic servant situation could be very much improved in that way, because I understand that in Britain they find it just as difficult to get domestic servants as we do. I believe the same condition prevails in France, where I read recently over seventy thousand Germans are doing essential work under the supervision of the French government. We have been getting a large number of immigrants from Holland, and they are very suitable, as are the Belgians, the Danes and others.
Now I should like to mention two other sources; that is, Germany and Italy. Although, as has been pointed out, they were recently enemy countries, nevertheless they possess a great reservoir of people who would be suitable for domestic service. I know from experience that girls and women in those countries are thoroughly trained as workers, and make good domestics not only in the city but also on the farms. I should point out that female help for the farms is a very serious problem with many people in Canada. It is almost impossible to get domestic servants to work on the farms. These people, I believe, could be obtained if a determined effort were made to get them. I am sure the reservoir is there, and the benefit that would accrue to this country if they could be brought here could hardly be measured. Therefore I would urge that the government give consideration to some method by which 55946-233

I should like to make a few observations while this subject is under consideration. I believe everyone in Canada was well pleased when the government decided to create the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. I am also satisfied that the people generally, and not only government supporters, were pleased when the present minister was chosen for this portfolio. We all agree that citizenship and immigration are of vital importance to the development and progress of our Canadian people. I am sure that it is a subject that requires careful study, because it is so vital to Canada. I am sure that in due time a vigorous, strong, and aggressive immigration policy will be announced for this dominion of ours. Most Canadians agree that we should have more immigrants in this country. Most people also agree that the number should be controlled, carefully screened and selected. Everyone agrees that we could not throw the borders of Canada open to mass immigration, because we could easily take in more people than we could assimilate. It is a well-known fact that when an enemy invaded China, the Chinese people soon assimilated the invader and they were all Chinese again. I believe it is vital that we have a studied immigration policy announced, and it should be fairly selective.
We only have a population of approximately fourteen million people. In view of the past records of our Canadian immigration policy, the number of immigrants should be arrived at by the departmental officials. I would say that from 100,000 to 200,000 would be a fair number at the start. Preference should be given to certain localities and certain races. We all agree that the British isles, France, and the United States should be considered, even if we have to subsidize those people to come here. We could help them with transportation and help them to settle. It might be worth while in the long run. In the riding which I have the honour to represent, Lambton-Kent, we have many representatives of the various races. In the early settlements there were Dutch, Belgians, Danish, and Ukrainian. These people settled in the Wallaceburg-Dresden area where they have raised certain special crops. They grow sugar beets and tobacco, and have made a great contribution to our welfare. I want to say a word or two in connection with the displaced persons, because we had a lot to do with trying to get people back to their homeland and placed in some situation where they could rehabilitate themselves. The UNRRA organization carried on a program of helping displaced persons until late in 1947, when that duty was taken over by the IRO. Among the various classes of displaced persons, the one that appealed to me particularly was the Russian. We knew them very well because, in many cases, we had them keeping our books and looking after our warehouses and supplies. They were people who had fled Russia in 1917 at the time of the revolution. They came to China, but did not want to take out citizenship papers in the Orient. They could not go back to their homeland. Late in 1947 an announcement was made that if these people went back to Russia they would be forgiven and full citizenship would be restored under the present regime. They would not take a chance on that. I remember one of the chaps particularly, who kept the records of our department, and he did want to go to Canada or some place like that. I believe these people are entitled to a great deal of consideration.
There is one more matter I should like to take up briefly. One of the problems that repeatedly faced me in China was that the Chinese people would say, "We like Canada pretty well, but Canada has always discriminated against our race." I said I did not think that could be correct, but they went on to tell me how they had been dis-
[Mr. MacKenzie.l

criminated against. I looked up some of the data on immigration into this country, and this is what I found out from the immigration department: From 1880 to 1890 many Chinese were brought into Canada as labourers for railway construction and other development work. From 1890 to 1900 some control of immigration was maintained by charging the Chinese $50 per head. This did not retard immigration, and in 1910 the head tax was raised to $500 each. That was continued until 1923 when the head tax was repealed, and an act was brought in called the Chinese Immigration Act. It became law, so it was impossible from 1923 on for any Chinese to come to this country, unless they came with shipping companies in the regular course of trade and commerce or came here as students attending university. This was the only immigration legislation that was ever enacted in Canada which applied to a particular race.
I well remember in 1947 when the announcement was headlined in the Chinese papers, both those printed in English and those printed in Chinese, that Canada had at last relaxed her immigration regulations and was allowing Chinese to enter. Upon making inquiries of the Canadian consul, I found it was not so great a step as had been reported, because all that had been done was to repeal the Chinese Immigration Act and put the Chinese on the same status as other Asiatics. Now the Chinese who have become Canadian citizens can bring in their wives and unmarried children up to the age of eighteen. From 1923 to 1947, or approximately twenty-five years, practically none of them came to this country. Very few Chinese had taken out citizenship papers. No purpose was served by taking them out, because a Chinese person could not go back and forward; so for the moment this relaxation did not do them very much good. Something else that was brought to my attention indirectly is that during all those years, from 1923 to 1947, the Japanese were allowed entry into Canada on an agreed or quota basis. In many cases they were admitted on the basis of up to 400 or 500 a year. This of course looked like discrimination. In view of the former discrimination against these people, I would suggest to the minister, as a good will gesture, that he at least allow the Chinese to bring their wives and unmarried children into Canada regardless of their age.
