This would not be a large number. It would be only a comparatively small number that would be affected.

May I say that I had to go to a foreign land before I fully realized what Canadian citizenship meant and what Canada should mean to the people here. I was asked many times what state 1 came from and when I said that I came from Canada, without hesitation and without any variation at all, these people all said that they would like to come to Canada, that they knew of no place in the world they would rather go. I think I said before and I say again that I do not believe there is any country in the world that stands in as high regard among the nations of the world as does Canada today. If we threw the regulations open we would have such a mass immigration here, if currency could be provided-and currency difficulties will clear away-that we could not possibly assimilate the immigrants. In my opinion most countries of the world appreciate Canada and what Canada has to offer more than do Canadians themselves. I would suggest to the minister that the policy we adopt for immigration into Canada must be a selective one. It must be carefully screened if we are going to maintain the high standards that we expect will be in effect in Canada in the years to come.

As far as I can understand from the speeches that have been given on this item, it appears that the majority of the members of this committee, whether they are Liberals or members of the opposition, realize that there is not a strong, concrete immigration policy being put forward by this government. I personally do not believe that it is one of those subjects about which you can lay down hard and fast rules. You cannot distribute human beings as you distribute freight, lumber or materials. Dealing with human beings requires a more flexible policy than dealing with natural resources. I do not underestimate the difficulties; they are great; but I think we could have a more concrete, specific and definite policy than we have at the present time. So far I can see, to date our piecemeal policy has been to bring individuals into Canada as individuals and to relax the regulations from time to time without any co-ordination between federal and provincial governments and other agencies, or without any relationship to the over-all economic development of Canada. I think that is the greatest weakness of the immigration policy or lack of policy on the

But this family, when they got there, felt lonely. The house provided by the farmer, and it was an excellent house, was a quarter of a mile away from neighbours. After staying for a week or so, this family became discontented and did not want to stay there any longer. Finally it was decided that nothing else could be done but to transport these people back to Nelson at public expense, transport them in a taxi to some point overnight at public expense, buy passages back to Ontario, buy tourist sleeper accommodation back to Ontario for the whole family, and bring them back to Ontario so that the government could start out again to locate this family which was not satisfied. In my opinion that situation would not occur if there were satisfactory coordination between the federal and provincial governments, with like co-ordination between the province and local agencies. Most Australians now living should survive to see their country inhabited by twenty million people. May Providence ordain it so. This will indeed be a tremendous accomplishment; it will be population increase on a scale never before attained, and hardly ever dreamed of in our land. It will match, and probably exceed, the great influxes of people that have attended gold rushes and the opening of rich territories in this and other parts of the world in the past. It will be all the more remarkable because it will take place in modern times. The days when immigrants would submit to herding aboard crowded and uncomfortable ships like human cattle are long past. The times are over when new settlers of any desirable kind would take their wives and families far from the comforts and amenities of life and allow their children to grow up without education or opportunities. Nobody could regret the passing of such conditions less than I do, but, of course, the modern necessity to bring immigrants in comfort to new lives of civilized usefulness makes our tasks immeasurably more complex and difficult than they would have been in earlier days.
The social and economic consequences to Australia of this great population drive will be vast. However desirable the immigrants may be, and however eager to welcome them the people of their new country may be, problems of absorption and assimilation can become very serious if there is not wise and careful planning in advance to solve or minimize them. I and my department, in close collaboration with other commonwealth departments, the governments of the states, and private industry, are now devoting an increasing amount of attention to such matters.

Mr. Chairman, for the sake of those who are tired and weary I shall state that I will be quite brief. I should like to take a moment or two to indicate my support of what has been said by other hon. members, notably the hon. member for Kamloops, about the great need for immigration and about our disappointment, which we do not fasten upon the shoulders of the minister, that the policy seems to be wanting. There are three main reasons that can be given for want of immigration in this country.

One may be on a rather high level which perhaps we do not urge very often, that we have a fine land here and we should not be so selfish as to keep it for ourselves. Some will regard that reason as being rather vague and I shall follow it by giving two reasons which are more definite and more self-regarding.
The second reason is that we need more people to help us pay for running this country. If he were here I am sure the Minister of Finance would agree with that because he has told us that our present expenses are at a practically irreducible minimum. Indeed he might have gone further and told us that they are going to rise considerably, as in all probability they will when we have dealt fully with the defence estimates. None of us is very happy about the taxes that must be paid at the moment and I am sure we would all welcome having a larger number of people in this country to help to carry the load.
The third reason is one which has been given quite often and it usually presses in on us more strongly as the years go by. This is that there is a military danger to all people who are occupying a land which may be coveted by others. That seemed remote years ago but now that the world has become so small we know that it is a thing that may happen.
I should like to take stock, as it were, of what you might call the composition of our population at the present moment. I suppose it is true to say that up to the beginning of this century we had the Anglo-Saxon and French streams moving side by side in Canada. It was not until the beginning of the century that we had any other very considerable element in our population. It is pleasant to reflect that as the years have gone by, particularly these last years, we have been making far greater progress in understanding each other. Perhaps that is due to the fact that in Europe the difficulties which used to separate France and England have been removed and they have been co-operating with each other with the fullest understanding for many years.
It is important to go back to the time just over fifty years ago when the Fashoda incident occurred in Africa. It might be interesting to recall an incident that occurred in the French chamber. A debate was going on to decide whether they should take steps against Great Britain in connection with this Fashoda incident. Tempers were running rather high when one witty member said, "After all, what is Britain? She is just a colony of France that did not succeed very well." It should be remembered that when we go far enough back we find that the Anglo-Saxon and Norman strains came from the same source. I do

We are learning to speak each other's language to a greater extent although we Anglo-Saxons have lagged behind in that regard. Nevertheless we are making progress and shall be able to do better.

I should like the minister to answer the question which was asked the other evening as to the position of some of our Canadian citizens who lost their citizenship rights by marrying people from other countries.

The hon. member for St. Paul's and the hon. member for Battle River are inquiring about the difficulty in which some of our Canadian girls find themselves with respect to their citizenship after having married, particularly during the war years. The answer is that amendments to the Canadian Citizenship Act were introduced in the other place today, I believe. At any rate they will be discussed there on Monday next, and after they have been passed will come here. I believe that problem will be solved if the house adopts those amendments.

The minister said that when we came to the individual items he would answer the questions that had been asked. I remember that the hon. member for Lake Centre made a speech on the matter of citizenship during the course of which he asked some questions, and I should think this would be the time to answer those questions, as well as one or two others that came up.

The hon. member for Lake Centre made specific reference to two points. In the first place he asked whether it would be desirable to issue a certificate to a person who filed a declaration of intention to become a Canadian citizen. I have looked into that suggestion and find that a receipt is issued to the applicant three months after he files his declaration of intention in the county or district court. That receipt is quite clear on its face that it is a 55916-234
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration receipt for a declaration of intention to become a Canadian citizen, and we feel that document should be sufficient for the purposes mentioned by the hon. member.
Then the hon. member suggested that in Canada we might adopt the idea of the freedom train, which they had in the United States. As he said, the freedom train cost something like $1,300,000, and that might be beyond the capacity of a department which gets only some $20 million odd to cover many services. However, the thought behind the freedom train is something I think we might very properly use in this country to increase the interest of our people in Canadian citizenship. We had a more or less minor experience of that kind with our own plan for the national capital which has gone around the country and in which our people have shown a great deal of interest. We are going to examine the possibility of arranging a collection of historic documents, much the same as they had in the United States, and other matters which should be drawn to the attention of the Canadian people in such a way as to create, not only in the newcomer to our country but in our own citizens as well, an interest in our history and traditions.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar made some mention of films, which perhaps we can deal with when he is in the chamber. In the citizenship branch we do issue a good many films and film strips, of which apparently he was not aware. There is an increasing demand for these, which we are supplying to anyone who asks for them. It is true that the hon. member made particular mention of a longer film dealing with our history, the cost of which according to our records would run to $10,000 or $12,000. We are concentrating rather on short strips for use in schools and other organizations, which in fact could be used almost anywhere. If it should happen that our estimates are increased certainly we will consider a film of considerable length at the cost I have mentioned, to present certain aspects in connection with citizenship.
I do not think there were any other questions, but if the hon. member for Calgary East has any of his own I shall be glad to answer them.

I suggested that a good deal more might be done in the matter of teaching citizenship in our schools; I thought that was one of the best ways of accomplishing something definite in this connection. I wonder if the department is taking any steps to obtain material which could be used in the schools to teach citizenship, and to get it into the hands of the teachers.

I did intend to refer to what the hon. member said in that connection. The citizenship branch is now publishing a number of booklets on the history of Canada and its institutions, more particularly designed for use in classes for newcomers. However, the booklets have been of such value and have created such interest in educational circles that the demand for them is increasing all the time. As the hon. member knows, schools and the like come under the provincial government, and we feel we should not enter the field unless by invitation of a particular province. I am happy to say that our relations with all the provincial governments and their educational branches are the very best, and at their request we do supply these booklets and will continue to do so, I hope in increasing numbers. As for the actual exercises in schoolrooms, we feel that is a matter for the provincial departments to control in their own way. I believe the hon. member is aware that this year we did begin certain exercises with respect to citizenship in relation to May 23. Again, however, those were wholly in the nature of an offer of assistance to the provincial departments of education in connection with the programs they might follow that day. This committee can take it for granted, Mr. Chairman, that we are only too happy to give any assistance through the citizenship branch for these purposes.

Has the
minister received a communication from the Canadian Club in Winnipeg concerning citizenship, and the granting of citizenship certificates?

I have received representations from several Canadian Clubs, not only in Winnipeg but in other centres, with respect to the observance of the granting of citizenship certificates, the kind of training which might be given to persons seeking citizenship, and the like. I appreciate very much these representations because we are anxious to assist the voluntary organizations, and particularly those in Winnipeg who, I might add, are very active in this respect. We will do what we can to accommodate our organization to the best facilities which can be given to the newcomer.

Can the

Mr. Chairman, I wrote to several of the persons who com-


municated on this subject, and I agreed with them that we should try to work out an acceptable method of dealing with the newcomers in the examination and granting of certificates. But I did point out that, beginning with the schools as I said before, we leave those to the provincial governments. In the courts, of course, the judges are in control of whatever procedure they wish to adopt. I would not care to say now what I said in my reply, because I have not got it here. I know what the hon. member has in mind, and we do hope to find a system whereby all the persons interested in the new citizens will be able to work together to carry out these programs in the best way.

I should like to say a word in appreciation of the Ontario Association for Adult Education, and what they have done in connection with displaced persons. The work has been almost entirely voluntary, and I know that in the district from which I come a school was taken over for two nights a week. A great deal of useful information was given, not only on the responsibilities of Canadian citizenship but also necessary information dealing with home economics and the problems of running a house. Having had in my employ a couple of displaced persons, may I say that the work being done in this connection was of tremendous assistance to these people. I strongly commend the work that is being done by this and other organizations.

I should like to ask the minister if the contract labour laws have been changed or cancelled. I received representations from someone in my constituency about some people who came in from the United States to do some work. Where labour was available, they refused to hire these people as they had their help, and it caused a lot of dissatisfaction.
Is the hon. member referring to people coming into Canada?
Yes.
Perhaps if the hon. member would give me the instance I could answer the question much better on another occasion. I am not familiar with it.

speechtext:
Can the minister now start
answering some of the many questions that he has before him? If I might suggest one, it would be the subject which I raised on April 21, and about which several other members have spoken, including the hon. member for Lambton-Kent today, namely, the question as to P. C. 2115.

The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre spoke about P. C. 2115 in the debate about a. month ago. The remarks he made were not those with which I might entirely agree, particularly when he refers to the misunderstanding which occurred over the repeal of the Chinese Immigration Act; because I do not agree with him that the statement made at that time was in any way misleading, although he and others perhaps did misunderstand it.
The present P. C. 2115 is an order in council passed, as I recall it, in September 1930 and it applies to all Asiatic people. In that connection, "Asiatic" refers to a geographical area lying roughly east of the Mediterranean, and within that area it provides that the only persons who may be admitted to Canada are the wives and unmarried children under eighteen of Canadian citizens. I realize that the hon. member thinks that this P. C. should be broadened to permit the admission to Canada of wives and children of persons from that area who are not Canadian citizens. I also realize that he and others have made representations that the age limit of eighteen for children might be increased. The present policy of the government, however, is to observe the order in council as it is, with one exception with which I think the committee is familiar; that is, an exception is made for a child to be brought forward up to nineteen if he or she is the sole remaining one of the family abroad.
The argument is made that this P. C. is discriminatory against those Canadians of Chinese origin. I must repeat that it is not a discrimination against them. They are covered by the same P. C. as other Asiatic peoples; and it is not correct to say that that is a peculiar discrimination against these people.

Perhaps I might give some figures to the committee. It must be remembered that, in the years before 1947, the Chinese Immigration Act did apply; and without going into the history of Chinese immigration into this country, as did the hon. member for Lambton-Kent tonight, we can start with 1947 and say generally that only 20 or 30 people of Chinese origin had been entering this country per year up to that time. The figure last year was just one or two over eight hundred. Up to the end of April this year something like four hundred have come in. At the same rate the figure for the whole of this year might reach twelve hundred. I think the committee will agree with me that until we see the limits of the movement to Canada of people of Chinese origin, we might well leave the P. C. as it is and consider if necessary a revision of it when the full facts of the movement are apparent.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I must say, Mr. Chairman,
that the figures the minister has given certainly put the government in a better light with respect to this matter than was formerly the case. The numbers used to be what one could count on the fingers of his hands. These figures of a few hundred seem to be a little bit more humane. I use that phrase particularly in relation to what should be our interest in family formations. Nevertheless, I hope the basic order will yet be changed.
Although I do not wish to pursue the argument with the minister at this time, in view of his statement that there was no reason for misunderstanding the position taken by the government back in 1947, I feel that I should put on record again at this point the statement at that time which was attributed to Mr. King, in a press release of January 27, 1947:
Mr. King said that, at an early stage of the session, the government intends to introduce a bill to repeal the Chinese Immigration Act which is regarded by the Chinese government as an exclusion act and in the nature of discrimination on grounds of race against a friendly and allied people. The effect of the repeal will be to remove all discrimination against the Chinese on account of race and to bring Chinese persons under the general provisions of the Immigration Act and no longer under legislation applying exclusively to persons of Chinese origin.
I see the minister nodding his head. In other words, he thinks that we both have a case for the position we are taking. I submit that the ordinary person, reading those words, would take from them the meaning that our Chinese Canadians took when that press release came to their attention in January, 1947, namely that the effect of the action to be taken by the government at the 1947 session of parliament would be to remove all discrimination against the Chinese on account of race. But we found that the latter words
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration in that statement, which were to the effect that they would no longer be under legislation applying exclusively to persons of Chinese origin, had the effect of putting them under an order in council which, it is true, does not apply exclusively to persons of Chinese origin, but it does apply to persons of Asiatic origin. This is where our Chinese Canadians and other Canadians who are interested in this matter feel that they were deceived. It cannot be said now that all discrimination against the Chinese on account of race has been abolished, as many Canadians feel it should be.

I should like to ask the minister a question with regard to Chinese students. Can Chinese students still come to Canada? I have in mind particularly doctors who want to interne in this country. I believe that formerly they could come to Canada, and I should like to know what the present status of that class of people is.

So far as the
Canadian government is concerned, the situation is the same as it has formerly been. Chinese students may come to Canada, to go to university. But there is this difficulty. At the moment one is not certain whether they can get the appropriate documents from the Chinese government so that they might return at the end of their period of education here.
What would be the position of a citizen of Hong Kong? Would he be able to come over here without this present difficulty that the minister mentions?

We took cognizance of the fact that there are a great many people in Hong Kong, commencing roughly last fall, and we did cut a certain amount of the regulations in the way of travel documents; but there are still some needed. If they obtain those, they can come forward; and in fact, they are coming forward from Hong Kong.
Can a doctor who has graduated from a Chinese university and wants to interne in Canada come to Canada at the present time as a citizen of Hong Kong?
Subject of course to the documents, yes.

Can the
minister tell us how the process of screening of potential immigrants is conducted in Europe?
I think the committee will understand the answer I am going to make. This is the kind of information that I do not think should be made public.

A most unsatisfactory answer.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
I realize that.

I am willing to admit that for security reasons certain things ought not to be told. In the past I have complained about a certain type of screening. I refer of course to those who have come into this country with false passports. I have tried to find out how these people's backgrounds were checked into because the passports were false. The only answer I am given is that it should not be made public. I think the answer is utterly absurd.

I was wondering whether the minister was in a position to make a statement with reference to the possible admission as immigrants of a certain Ukrainian group now in the United Kingdom and who formerly went under the name of "division Halychyna." This group as a military unit was originally formed during the war on Soviet territory. It was motivated by a desire to form a nucleus of a military group around which other military units would centre for the creation of an independent Ukraine. They wanted to break away from the soviet tyranny. In the turmoil this military division found itself under German jurisdiction. That they detested the nazis as much as they hated the communists is indicated by the fact that immediately upon contact with the allies they surrendered to the United States army. They then became prisoners of war and were taken to England. After staying in England for a while they were released to work as free citizens. I understand that a lot of them are anxious to reach the shores of Canada and to settle here. I am sure they would make desirable citizens if they came into this country.

The Ukrainian persons mentioned by the hon. member for Vegreville had the history he has given. When they were taken prisoners of war by our troops in Italy it was recognized by the allied commander that there were special circumstances in connection with that division because they were not treated entirely as other prisoners of war were. They have been in England since the spring or fall of 1945. We have investigated not individuals but the group as a whole, and we are quite prepared to accept them provided they come within the ordinary rules with respect to immigrants; that is, they might be agricultural workers, settlers, and the like. May I express the hope, since it may be the only opportunity I have to refer to the speech of the hon. member for Vegreville, that their sons might turn out just as he has.

I believe we are on item 51; at least we are talking about that item. Tuesday night I asked the minister whether he would tell the committee what the government's present policy is in respect of immigration from Italy, and whether it is expected that the policy may be changed in the near future. Can the minister make a statement now?

Immigration from Italy is on the same basis as it was prior to the war, since we have a peace treaty with Italy and have restored the normal relationships. Italians may come provided they are close relatives within the description found in P.C. 2743, and also agricultural workers and settlers.

Can the minister make a statement with regard to the position of Germans? I understand the governing factor is that we have not yet got a peace treaty with Germany. I must say that that seems a bit hard on a number of Germans, and people who are now classified as German nationals although racially they are not Germans. It seems a bit hard on them because it is hardly their fault. A number of them would make good citizens. I hope the minister will understand that I am not suggesting a complete relaxation of all the investigations and safeguards which now exist against the admission of people of nazi tendencies and symptoms. What I am suggesting is merely that the fact that we have not yet been able to complete a peace treaty with Germany because of Russia should no longer be allowed to prevent these Germans and other Europeans, who would make desirable immigrants in accordance with the present security standards, from coming into this country. Can the minister say anything with regard to that?

Before the minister replies, perhaps I might ask a supplementary question. I hold a newspaper clipping in my hand dated June 5. It was taken from the Toronto Star and it says that Germany asks Canada to take 500,000 Sudetens. This dispatch is headed "Bonn, Germany", and says that mass settlement of 500,000 Germans in Canada is being sought by the west German government.
I should like to know if they have made a formal application to the Canadian government to take that number. If so, has the request been considered in any way? What has been done about it?

What is the difference
between Germans and the Volksdeutsche?
Has the minister at his fingertips the number of Germans who have come into Canada since the regulations changed?
No, because that was in March. I can give the April figure, but that is all I can give.
What was the April figure?

In the meantime I will answer the hon. member for York West. The Volksdeutsche are persons of German ancestry who, by my description at any rate, were living outside the limits of Germany prior to the war, persons in Poland, the Baltic states, Czechoslovakia, and the like.
I just wanted that on the record.

I have a special case to refer to in my constituency of Cumberland. German settlers came to that county after the first great war, Mr. and Mrs. Ernest Woock. They have proved themselves to be the highest type of citizen. They settled on a farm and enlarged their acreage. They have recently enlarged it by another eighty acres, and have made a success of farming operations. They recently became Canadian citizens. He was fconscripted in the first great war and served as a German. There are no children. They have a nephew who served in the last great war in France, and he is still in France. They have made application that he be allowed to come to Canada to assist them on the farm. They wish to make him their heir. This is a special case that should have the sympathetic consideration of the department.
I should like to know if the policy of the department has been changed in order to permit such an applicant to come to this country. Has the minister the authority to give such special permission or would it be done by order in council? The uncle and aunt who live in Cumberland have been
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration ready to advance the necessary funds for his passage and other expenses, but they were not accepted by the steamship company and he has not yet received permission to come. These settlers in Cumberland have proved to be excellent citizens and they have certificates as being the best citizens in the community. They have evidence of their high standing as citizens from the manager of the bank and I think it would be most desirable that in this special case permission be granted so that this boy can come to Canada.

Without going into the details of this particular case, a nephew would not be admissible. It is only close relatives who are admissible and that does not extend to nephews unless they happen to be orphans. If my hon. friend will speak to me later about the case I shall look into it and give him a firm answer.
To answer the question asked by the hon. member for Moose Jaw, there were 641 persons of German origin who came in in April. Those would not all be from Germany as it is the racial origin, not necessarily the place whence they came, that is indicated.

There have been a number of speeches on immigration since these estimates were first introduced in April and I had hoped that the minister would make something in the nature of a general statement and answer the considerable number of questions, either direct or implied, contained in the speeches. I think in almost every case the tenor of the speech was disappointment that the number of people coming into this country as immigrants has been steadily falling during recent months or during last year.as compared with the year before.
Nearly every speaker wanted to know what means were going to be taken to reverse that trend and to increase immigration into the country in pursuance of the policy announced back in 1947. We have not had anything so far along that line. It has been impossible to ascertain what there is in prospect to increase the number of immigrants from the British isles, which number has been decreasing materially during recent months owing to exchange difficulties particularly. We have not been told that there are any prospects of overcoming those exchange difficulties. Is the minister prepared to make a general statement in reply to the general criticism from all parts of the house, and will he indicate whether any specific steps are in prospect to reverse this trend?

Mr. Chairman, I think perhaps I might avoid making an extended statement, but a number of specific


this country and the hon. member for Kootenay West gave us the details of the Australian plan to assist immigration. Recently, at any rate, this country has not provided subsidized transportation as is done in Australia. I have read the booklets and other publications which are published in Australia in the interests of obtaining immigration, which were referred to by my hon. friend.
The Australian government is spending quite a considerable amount of money in advertising, but I repeat that the crux of the matter is the exchange difficulty. People will come here if they can bring their money, and until that problem is solved there is no point in spending large sums of money on publishing booklets and distributing them to people who could not react to them in any event.
When the leader of the opposition spoke in this debate a month ago he went into considerable details about the difficulties in London in connection with applications, processing and so on. With a good deal of what he said I am in complete agreement. It would be desirable to have all these various activities under one roof so that the intending immigrant could come to town and perhaps in one day get through most of the necessary work under the one roof. We hope to improve our facilities in the very near future in London and other parts of the United Kingdom. I do not believe there are any other specific questions, but if I have overlooked any I shall be glad to discuss them.
Can the minister supplement the reply he gave to the hon. member for Macleod as to the number of Italians who came in under this regulation during January, February, March or April of this year?

Up to the end of
April there were 2,294.

There is one point on which I should like to have the minister express his view. It has to do with the service at the border points. I raise this matter because of an item in the press some two years ago about several hundred United States cars being turned back at a border point in British Columbia. This action of course affected a great many people and also affected our tourist dollars. What I have in mind is that I understand that at certain border points at some times the United States combine the customs and immigration officers, and one man takes the responsibility for discharging the duties of both in order to expedite the entry of the person or car as the case may be.
I feel rather keenly about this matter because it is quite important that when our United States friends come to Canada they

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
should not be unnecessarily delayed for any unusual length of time with the result that a lot of them turn back and do not . come into Canada' because of the delay at the border. We depend on the immigration and customs officials a great deal to boost our tourist industry because they are the first Canadians whom the Americans contact when they enter our country. We expect a great deal of them, and I have never been satisfied that those at the border points are being compensated sufficiently for the responsibilities that they have to assume and what is demanded of them. I should like to have the minister comment as to whether or not in the rush seasons we could introduce something along the same line as they have on the other side in order to expedite the entry of United States people into Canada.

Mr. Chairman, the mixing of customs and immigration officers that the hon. member has mentioned is on an experimental basis in the United States at the moment, and we are keeping in touch with the situation to see if it is satisfactory. We do of course put on extra help during the summer months, and particularly when a large number of tourists are expected. Nevertheless I agree with the hon. member that we should give the best reception to these people that we possibly can. I think I mentioned in my earlier statement that we checked into Canada something like 39 million people last year. Of course a great many of them were commuters and the like, but if there are any opportunities for improving the facilities for receiving these people, particularly in my hon. friend's riding, I shall be glad to consider them. At any rate I can assure him that during the summer months I am going to visit some of these points myself to see if we can improve the facilities.

In the details for immigration on page 103 there is an amount of $242,000 for overtime, which is the same as last year. Was that amount actually spent last year, or was it just an estimate, and what is the situation this year?
Is the hon. member objecting to the fact that we are not spending more?
No. I was wondering how the amount of $242,000 for overtime was made up and why you call it overtime. Is it for overtime work, is it allowed in place of leave, or what is it?

At the immigration points the staff work overtime to complete the week's work, and we pay them on a pro rata basis in the same manner as we have
in previous years. This represents the same amount of overtime, perhaps with a larger staff, but we prefer to do it that way rather than to put on extra staff for the small amount of overtime that must be worked.
I wondered why it was exactly the same as last year.
That means we have the same staff.

I should like to ask the minister whether any special effort is being made to encourage migration from the United States, particularly from the middle west. We have large areas in the Peace river country and elsewhere in the north, and settlers from Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and the middle west seem to do very well there with the cheap land that we have in the northwestern part of Canada. According to one very good authority I am told that we can finish a hog in the Peace river country at 5 cents per pound.
Let us cut the price of bacon right away.

You can see the possibilities in the use of that land by men who know about hogs and corn, how to put the two together and how to develop prosperous mixed farming projects. It is all very well to talk about bringing in men from Denmark. Among the best settlers we have had in Canada, and particularly in Alberta, were dairymen from Denmark who came here and assisted in developing co-operative creameries, cheese factories, and so on. We have had good men from Sweden. I can point to a good many people all through the northwest with prosperous farms, and some of them right in this house tonight, who originated in Sweden.
We have had good men from Norway, but after all we want our own Anglo-Saxon stock to be given an opportunity in the northwest where these new areas are waiting to be settled. We want Englishmen, Irishmen, Scotsmen, and let us not forget our United States friends. We had 90,000 Americans on the Alaska highway to build a lifeline to the Alaska perimeter, and we did not do anything about giving them any land. If I had been in the position of the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King I would have given each of them 160 acres of land in that country, but we did not do it. The land is there, the opportunity is there, and we should invite settlement of those areas. The French Canadian people of the province of Quebec should

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration be invited to go to northeastern British Columbia and northern Alberta. I regret that the people of Ontario refuse to turn their attention to the possibilities of that great country. United States people are well qualified to settle there. They know about tractors, and they know the mysteries of hog farming. They understand the mysteries of hog raising; they know how to build silos; they know how to clear land. Let us get as many Americans as we possibly can to come in along the Alaska highway and into these new areas.

Has the minimum wage scale been increased within the last two or three years? In other words, at what rate is a new employee engaged, and how much higher is that rate than it was last year or the year before?

The immigration officers are in the same position as other civil servants. They have received their annual increases and the special increases which have been granted civil servants from time to time. If my hon. friend has any particular appointment in mind I shall be glad to give him the precise figure.
Let us say you take on a man, a novice, as an inspector at a port. I assume he is paid a minimum wage, and that is the amount I should like to have.
The minimum is

And what was it three or
four years ago?

I will have to
look that up and let my hon. friend know.

Mr. Chairman, just briefly
I should like to pay tribute to the director of immigration, Mr. Jolliffe, who has held that position for a great number of years. Certainly in all the dealings I have had with him and all the dealings anyone else I know has had with him he has gone to the greatest trouble to settle our problems. The number of people who are in Canada today through the humanitarian efforts of this notable servant of Canada is very large, and I wanted to pay this small tribute to him at this time.
Now I want to ask the minister how the IRO is going to be supported next year, after the funds are exhausted. I understand that officially the IRO will wind up next year, or even within the present fiscal year. I have several questions to ask, but the first is, what is the policy of the government concerning the operations of the IRO?
My next question has to do with the displaced persons' camps in both the American

and British sectors of Germany, where there are still large numbers of people. These unfortunates are perhaps in an older age group than those who emigrated to Australia and Canada in the last few years, but we cannot consider them an indigestible group. Something must be done to solve that problem before the major question of a peace treaty with Germany can be worked out. On our responsibility as belligerents, and our responsibility from the humanitarian point of view, we must realize that there are in Germany today many thousands of people for whom work cannot be found there; but there is work for them in Canada. They are not like the young, virile people we have received from the displaced persons' camps in years gone by; still there is work for them, particularly in our large institutions. For example, I understand that a short time ago the Toronto General hospital was so short of assistance that a great many rooms had to be closed. They had not enough nurses; they had not enough ward assistants to service that great institution completely. To what extent that was true I cannot say positively, but certainly I was told of someone who could not get in the hospital because, while the rooms were available, the service could not be provided. In these camps are many people who could do ward work and the various other duties that have to be performed in these great institutions. In addition there is still a great unsatisfied demand throughout Canada for domestic servants, and I am sure that many of these people, who are perhaps in their fifties, could give satisfactory service. I believe it is our responsibility to see that something is done about them.
I now come to the people whom the Netherlands are so anxious to send to Canada for farm work. I want to ask the minister whether any special scheme has been worked out with specific reference to citizens of the Netherlands for farm work in Canada. I remember that some years ago there was a system of assisted immigration for citizens of Switzerland who came to Canada, and particularly to Manitoba. That scheme was extraordinarily satisfactory. As a matter of fact I believe the chief surgeon of- one of the principal hospitals in Winnipeg is the son of a man who came out as one of those Swiss immigrants.
I repeat that the problem of the displaced persons is not solved. I am free to admit that we in Canada have done our share and perhaps more, certainly as compared with the United States, but the problem still exists. There is no use shutting our eyes to it, because it is still there. Before any satisfactory solution of the problem of Germany can be worked out some solution must

be found to the problem of the refugees who have flooded into that country. There is work for those people in Canada today, of the sort I have suggested. Perhaps they would not be able to do active work in construction jobs or on the farms, but there is work here for people who would be prepared to help with the domestic work involved in operating pur great institutions. That is one thing. With regard to the question of importing brains, I might say that if there is one thing that was done that was not so advantageous, it was the bringing to Canada of a number of displaced persons who were extremely well educated. A great number of professional people, such as university professors, surgeons, doctors, and other highly skilled people have come to Canada and gone into domestic service for one year. After a year in domestic service, or the first service they entered upon coming to Canada, they left that service. That is quite understandable.
Does the hon. member know of any of them who stayed the year?

Yes, they stayed a year, but not one d.p. couple stayed more than their contract year. I suggest there is still a demand for this type of labourer, but the displaced persons whom we brought out did not stay. They all went into other, perhaps more remunerative work than that for which they first came out. I suggest to the minister that is a problem that is still unsolved. There are many men, women, and in many cases children, who are still in these camps. Something will have to be done about them. They cannot remain where they are. I feel that through the continued operation of the IRO, or some other international organization, we should co-operate in every way possible. I do want to suggest to the minister that there are great opportunities for displaced persons in Canada, particularly in those fields in which we are short of labour.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has asked a specific question as to what we are doing about the continuation of the operation of the IRO. Of course the IRO is not under my department.
I realize that.

There is a vote under external affairs, item 84, which provides for about $2 million as our contribution to the IRO. This organization was to wind up on July 31, but I believe it is being continued for some months in view of the difficulty my hon. friend has mentioned. A representative of the IRO was here early in the winter, and we discussed with him some
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration of the problems. I think I can assure the hon. member that, as I said before, we shall continue to take an interest in these people, and to share in the solution of the problem he has stated.
With respect to the Netherlands question,
I think I covered that and I do not want to quote myself.
There are so many committee meetings that I missed what the minister said.

Earlier in this discussion I said that there were about 3,000 Netherlands citizens who came here in 1947; 7,000 in 1948; 7,000 in 1949; and approximately 4,500 to this date this year. In almost every instance they are agricultural workers coming to this country under the Netherlands foundation. I might add that we are particularly pleased with this movement of Netherlands citizens, and we hope it will continue.
I should like to ask the minister how many persons Canada deported last year.
I shall look that up and let the hon. member have the figure.

With respect to displaced persons, I hope I may give the house some information regarding an experiment which was made about ten years ago in bringing German settlers, that is displaced persons from the Sudetenland area to Canada. Those people were placed in my riding at Tupper Creek, which is near Dawson Creek. Some three hundred families in all were brought to Canada. They received from the British government approximately $1,500 in funds which were locked up in one of those countries from which they came-I mean their credits were standing in Britain and their money was in Czechoslovakia or some of the other areas. Those people came to Canada. They received $1,500 per family and took up land which was not considered by the average Canadian as very good land.
They have been in Canada ten years. They did not know our language. They knew nothing of our laws or our customs. What has been the result over the ten years? A community of happy, prosperous people who have contributed a great deal to the economy of that part of Canada. They have gone into dairying; they have cleared land; they have built homes. Those Germans, although many of us would say they are aliens, and possibly enemy aliens, are today part of our Canadian citizenship. They are giving a good account of themselves. I suggest to this house that is a test tube experiment. It is our responsibility to work out,
3702	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration on a much larger scale, that successful experiment which has been carried out at Tupper Creek and Dawson Creek.

Mr. Chairman, as indicated some time ago, the thing which chiefly concerns me, so far as immigration is concerned, is that the number of immigrants has been steadily dropping. I believe the same view was expressed by many other speakers. The minister has indicated that some plans are under way to try to solve the exchange difficulties which prevent more immigrants coming to this country from the British isles. Can he tell us if any plans are under consideration, or if the department has any other ideas as to how this downward trend in immigration could be stopped and an upward trend started? I think that is what most of us want to know so far as immigration is concerned.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think I can say it differently than I did a moment ago. The exchange difficulties consequent upon the depreciation of the pound are, in fact, the problem which has to be solved. As I indicated before, I do not feel I should try now to explain my own thoughts as to how it could be done because they are not crystallized. But I assure the hon. member that should we come to a solution we will announce it at once.

I should like to ask a question or two, and put a suggestion before the minister with respect to these regulations we are discussing which stand in the way of the admission of certain European nationals in the hope that he might consider the relaxation of at least one category of relatives. In many cases the husband has been a war casualty, and the brother of a relative in Canada. The wife and children of the man who was the war casualty are not admissible to Canada, and the children particularly are not admissible unless they are orphans. In this case the wife is not a sister but a sister-in-law, and I wonder if the minister would consider the relaxation of the regulations, at least to the extent of including, in the admissible class, sisters-in-law and their children, who would be blood relations to the people in Canada.
I would be glad to consider that. I take it the hon. member means that the applicant in Canada would be able to provide satisfactory settlement?
Yes.
I shall be glad to give consideration to that. The hon. member for Selkirk asks about the number of deportations. There were 416 for the fiscal year ended March 31.

You have increased your staff. Is there any reason for that? You have increased them from eight to nine. Four hundred and twenty do not seem to be many people for nine officers to handle. Do they do anything else? Is their sole job that of throwing people out of Canada? I could throw 420 out myself.

Shall
the item carry?
Carried.
Mr. Chairman-
Tell me something about it. I want to know.
Order.

I have one particular question with regard to the details. I see that for publications and advertising the amount is $158,000 which is up from $85,000 last year. Can the minister explain what the reason is for that and what these publications and advertising consist of?

They actually provide for the advertising which we hope to do should we overcome the difficulties we have just been discussing. In particular we propose to make a number of motion pictures depicting scenes in Canada which would be attractive to prospective immigrants and also two publications which are known as "This is Canada" and "Canada Descriptive Atlas." The purpose is to increase the interest of persons who might come to this country.

Is the minister able to make a general statement covering information to which reference was made earlier, that the number of immigrants has declined over the last three years by nearly 50 per cent and the cost of administration in Canada-that is, in the first two items I quoted, departmental administration and field inspectional service in Canada-have increased in the same period by approximately 25 per cent?

The increase in staff is largely due to the necessity of having inspectional service in Canada. The requirements of inspection have been increased in the last two or three years and for that reason the staff has been increased accordingly. As the hon. member pointed out, there has not been an increase in the staff abroad; but I think he will agree with me that a good base at home is desirable before we launch into the other branch of attracting immigration.

May I just point out that the same provision, or the same type of inspection facilities and charges by the labour

department under this heading is also increased, so that the two departments are sharing the costs of follow-up and so on and investigation in Canada; and I cannot see any justification as yet for that substantial increase in costs when at the same time our immigration is falling and facilities overseas for arranging for immigration are apparently being reduced, if one can judge by the reduction in the estimates there. If the number were increasing, I would agree with the minister; but unless he can show that we are preparing for a program of increased immigration, I cannot agree with him that there is justification for that increase.
I have no hesitation in saying that we are; and I have just given an indication of the increase in one particular item.
Have any studies been made by the department as to the capacity of Canada to absorb immigration?
As to the question of publicity, I suppose that the hon. member for Kamloops refers to advertising, does he, and propaganda?
I have not mentioned it.

The time is now ripe for this country within reason to do considerable publicity and advertising of the resources and possibilities of the country. At the present time we are hosts to the commonwealth press conference. In the city of Ottawa tonight we have some of the leading publishers of Britain and of the commonwealth countries. I would suggest to you that they are unpaid ambassadors of good will to Canada, going out to the seven seas to tell of the possibilities of this country. I particularly refer to Sir Harry Brittain, a distinguished man who was in Winnipeg in 1909, who was himself a settler in Manitoba and who brought many settlers into certain areas in Alberta at that time. I say that intelligent and constructive publicity at this time throughout the world is one of the best investments that the Canadian people could make.

No, it is
not carried. I am still waiting for an answer.

We have conducted conferences, as was suggested by the hon. member for Kootenay West, with the various provincial organizations having to do with immigration. With them and through
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration our own settlement service we are studying the question of how many people we might settle here and there throughout the country. Those studies have not been concluded; but that is the only actual study that has been made or is being made at the moment.

I have a keen interest in immigration. By consulting my files I find that, from 1940 up to the present time, I have spoken twice on the matter. My only purpose in rising now is to call to the attention of the committee the speech I made on Wednesday, April 3, 1946. As it represents entirely the opinions I still have on the matter, I will not repeat it. I am just rising for the purpose of calling that speech to the attention of the committee.
Have you any copies of it?
I should like to ask one question. Why are the expenses in this item so high? I think the travelling expenses are $261,000 and the total travelling expenses for the whole department are $750,000.

In answer to the first part of the question, my recollection is that there were 106,000 different calls made by our inspectors on persons in Canada who had applied for persons abroad. That is the reason for the travelling costs. For that reason we have particularly high expenses for travelling. Every application has to be considered in the office and perhaps an inspection made out in the country by someone with respect to the settlement facilities.

Item agreed to.
Immigration branch-
52.	Field and inspectional service, Canada, $3,732,561.

On this particular item
there comes up the question which was asked particularly by the hon. member for Kamloops in connection with the fact that the major portion of the money spent with regard to immigration is spent under this particular vote, $3,733,000, whereas, as to foreign service-that is on people outside Canada whose primary duty is to get immigration into the country-we spent only $881,000. It seems to me that there is a disproportion there and that if we are going to get immigration we should have more people abroad, should be sending more people there for that purpose, and should be spending more money there instead of spending the greatest part of the money which we spend on immigration on people within Canada. That is just one general criticism of this thing which strikes one. I should like the minister to make some comment on that matter. While I am on my feet, and in order to save time, may I ask
3704	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration another question. There is an item here of $220,000 for travelling expenses this year; it was $198,000 last year. I wonder what the reason is for that. What is the necessity for such a large amount for travelling expenses in this department within Canada? We have these immigration officers stationed all across the dominion. I cannot quite see why there should be such a large amount necessary for travelling expenses?

I thought we
had passed that item after I had given the hon. member for Queens the explanation with respect to travelling expenses. We are on item 53, are we not?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Item 52.

I gave an
explanation of the number of calls made in Canada by the inspectional service. They were 106,000 last year. I think these are calls made by our inspectors at the homes of persons who have asked for a particular immigrant. For that reason we have the $240,000. On the other question of the disproportion of expenses between the staff in Canada and that abroad, I have already pointed out that we have to maintain ports of entry in Canada for the purpose of looking after not only the immigrants as such but also persons who commute, tourists and the like, and we have a much larger staff in Canada than we ever will have abroad for that reason.

Can the minister give the
information I asked for?

I did not quite
understand what my hon. friend wanted. I understood that he said we had nine persons employed to deport people.
Of all people I do not know why the minister should not understand me.
It is not that, I did not hear.

I want to know , why it was necessary to have an increase of from eight to nine deportation officers. The minister told me that 420 people had been deported. I think it is most unreasonable. Can the minister explain to me why it was necessary to have the increase? That is all I want to know. There has been an average of one and a half deportations a day. Does it take nine men to deport one and a half persons?

There is a good deal more to it than that. Four hundred and sixteen were deported. Well and good; but there are a good many more who are being held pending deportation or consideration of


appeals which they make to the minister. We have found it necessary to add one more to the staff.
How many permanent organizations are there? What is the set-up of these organizations abroad covered by this item?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: We have not passed item 52 yet.
Can the minister give a break-down of the reasons for the deportation of these 416 people?

The reasons are published in the annual report for the fiscal year. I admit that it is not published1 yet. I would hope that my hon. friend would not expect me to go through the 416 cases now and give him the reason in each case.

I do not
expect it now, but I hope to be supplied with the information.
I should imagine that there is no particular pattern. I could not say that 200 were deported for the same reason. I could detail it but I would hope that my hon. friend would not ask for it.
Any particular reason?
Why does the minister not deport Paul Jokelson of Montreal and Camet of Winnipeg?

Item agreed to.
Immigration branch-
53.	Field and inspectional service, abroad. $881,792.
I want to ask the minister what permanent organizations he has and where they are situated outside Canada.

There are not so
many. I could run through them quickly. In the British isles they are at Belfast, Dublin, Glasgow, Liverpool and London.
Can the minister say how many people are at each of these places, and whether they have a complete processing staff in each case?

May I complete the list? On continental Europe, Salsburg, Brussels, Paris, Karlsruhe, Athens, Rome, The Hague, Stockholm, Berne; there is also Hong Kong. I will give my hon. friend a statement of the number of employees in each case.

I have one question. I see an item here for repatriation of wives and dependents of members of the Canadian armed forces, $3,000. It was $5,000 last year. I would have thought that all wives and dependents of members of the Canadian armed forces would have been repatriated by

this time. I was rather surprised to see that item. I wonder whether the minister can tell us what the reason is that we still have a vote of that kind. How many of these people were repatriated last year, and were covered by the $5,000?
We still have a few that we pay to bring here, and I think that is all that needs to be said.

I do not think that is an answer. I asked, what is the reason that we are still repatriating wives of members of the Canadian armed services. I would have thought they would have all been here before this time. How many were repatriated last year?

I am informed the reason is that in some cases they have not been able to make arrangements up until now for settlement in this country and they are still coming forward, and we have a vote to cover the cost. On another occasion I will give my hon. friend the figures of those brought in last year.
The minister was going to give me a break-down of the stations abroad.
I will do that.
